Hydrolysis of an ester with dilute acid is an irreversible reaction.
back:
**False.**

Acid hydrolysis of an ester is **reversible** — an equilibrium is established. Only alkaline hydrolysis is irreversible.

front: When propanol reacts with ethanoic acid, the ester formed is **..........**. The first part of the name comes from the **..........** .
back: When propanol reacts with ethanoic acid, the ester formed is **propyl ethanoate**. The first part of the name comes from the **alcohol**.

front: What products are formed when an ester undergoes alkaline hydrolysis, and what additional step is needed to obtain the carboxylic acid?
back: Alkaline hydrolysis produces a **sodium carboxylate salt** and an **alcohol**. The carboxylate ion (-COO<sup>-</sup>) must then be **acidified** (e.g. with HCl) to produce the free carboxylic acid.

front:
**True or False?**

Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester is irreversible because the carboxylate salt formed cannot readily re-form the ester.
back:
**True.**

Alkaline hydrolysis is irreversible. The ester is fully broken down to a sodium carboxylate salt and an alcohol. Acid hydrolysis, by contrast, is reversible.

front: Define **acid hydrolysis of esters**.
back: An **acid hydrolysis of esters** is a reversible reaction in which an ester is heated under reflux with dilute acid, reforming the carboxylic acid and alcohol in an equilibrium mixture.

front: After alkaline hydrolysis of an ester, the sodium carboxylate salt must be **..........**  with an acid to convert the **..........**  ion into a carboxylic acid.
back: After alkaline hydrolysis of an ester, the sodium carboxylate salt must be **acidified** with an acid to convert the **carboxylate** ion into a carboxylic acid.

front: Ethanol and propanoic acid react together. Name the ester formed and the small molecule eliminated.
back: The ester formed is **ethyl propanoate**. The small molecule eliminated is **water** (H<sub>2</sub>O), as this is a condensation reaction.

front: Define **amine**.
back: An **amine** is a compound containing the -NH<sub>2</sub> functional group, formed by nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane with ammonia.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to produce an amine from a halogenoalkane?
back: The halogenoalkane is heated under pressure with **ethanolic ammonia** (NH<sub>3</sub> dissolved in ethanol).

front:
**True or False?**

The nitrogen atom in ammonia acts as a nucleophile because it has a lone pair of electrons.
back:
**True.**

The lone pair on the nitrogen of NH<sub>3</sub> attacks the partial positive carbon of the C-X bond in the halogenoalkane, replacing the halogen in a nucleophilic substitution reaction.

front: In the nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane by NH<sub>3</sub>, the **..........**  atom of ammonia attacks the **..........**  charged carbon of the C-X bond.
back: In the nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane by NH<sub>3</sub>, the **nitrogen** atom of ammonia attacks the **partially positive** charged carbon of the C-X bond.

front: Why does the C-X bond in a halogenoalkane have a partial positive charge on the carbon?
back: The halogen atom is more **electronegative** than carbon, so it draws electron density away from the C-X bond towards itself. This gives the carbon a partial positive charge (δ+) and the halogen a partial negative charge (δ-).

front:
**True or False?**

Reacting bromoethane with ethanolic ammonia under heat and pressure produces ethylamine and hydrobromic acid.
back:
**True.**

The NH<sub>3</sub> substitutes the Br in bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution, forming ethylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) and hydrobromic acid (HBr) as the byproduct.

front: Amines are produced from halogenoalkanes by **..........**  substitution, in which the halogen is replaced by an **..........**  group.
back: Amines are produced from halogenoalkanes by **nucleophilic** substitution, in which the halogen is replaced by an **amine** group.

front: Define **nucleophile**.
back: A **nucleophile** is an electron-pair donor that attacks electron-deficient (partial positive) atoms. The nitrogen lone pair in NH<sub>3</sub> acts as a nucleophile in the production of amines.

front: Why is an ethanolic solution of ammonia used rather than an aqueous solution to produce amines from halogenoalkanes?
back: Aqueous ammonia contains water, which can act as a nucleophile and cause **hydrolysis** of the halogenoalkane, producing an **alcohol** as a competing product. Using **ethanolic ammonia** removes water, ensuring NH<sub>3</sub> is the only nucleophile present and the reaction selectively produces the **amine**.

front: Define **nitrile**.
back: A **nitrile** is a compound containing the -CN functional group, prepared by nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane with ethanolic KCN.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to convert a halogenoalkane into a nitrile?
back: The halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with an **ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide (KCN in ethanol)**. The CN<sup>-</sup> ion acts as the nucleophile.

front:
**True or False?**

The reaction of a halogenoalkane with ethanolic KCN increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom.
back:
**True.**

The CN<sup>-</sup> ion adds a carbon atom to the chain as it substitutes the halogen. This makes the reaction useful for chain extension in synthesis.

front: Hydroxynitriles contain both a **..........**  group and a **..........**  group, typically attached to the same carbon atom.
back: Hydroxynitriles contain both a **-OH** group and a **-CN** group, typically attached to the same carbon atom.

front: Describe the two-step mechanism by which HCN adds to ethanal to form a hydroxynitrile.
back:
**Step 1:** The CN<sup>-</sup> ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanal, forming a negatively charged intermediate.

**Step 2:** The oxygen of the intermediate is protonated by H<sup>+</sup> (from HCN, water or dilute acid) to give **2-hydroxypropanenitrile**.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrolysis of a nitrile does not change the number of carbon atoms in the chain.
back:
**True.**

Hydrolysis converts the -CN group into -COOH without adding or removing carbon atoms. The chain length is preserved, unlike nitrile formation which adds one carbon.

front: Nitriles can be hydrolysed by dilute **..........**  to form a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt, or by dilute **..........**  followed by acidification to form a carboxylic acid.
back: Nitriles can be hydrolysed by dilute **acid** to form a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt, or by dilute **alkali** followed by acidification to form a carboxylic acid.

front: Define **hydroxynitrile**.
back: A **hydroxynitrile** is a compound with both -OH and -CN groups on the same carbon, formed by nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde or ketone.

front: Why is the use of ethanolic KCN (rather than aqueous KCN) important when making a nitrile from a halogenoalkane?
back: Using **aqueous** KCN risks forming an **alcohol** (via hydrolysis) instead of the nitrile. **Ethanolic** KCN ensures the nucleophilic substitution proceeds to give the nitrile product.

front: Define **addition polymerisation**.
back: An **addition polymerisation** is a reaction in which many monomers containing at least one C=C double bond join together to form long polymer chains as the only product.

front: What bond change occurs in the monomer during addition polymerisation?
back: The **π-bond** in the C=C double bond breaks. The monomers then link together to form new **C-C single bonds**, producing the polymer chain.

front:
**True or False?**

Addition polymerisation produces two products: the polymer and a small molecule such as water.
back:
**False.**

Addition polymerisation produces only one product — the polymer. No small molecules are released, which distinguishes it from condensation polymerisation.

front: In addition polymerisation, the small reactive molecules that join together are called **..........**. The long-chain molecule they form is called a **...........**.
back: In addition polymerisation, the small reactive molecules that join together are called **monomers**. The long-chain molecule they form is called a **polymer**.

front: Define **repeat unit**.
back: A **repeat unit** is the smallest group of atoms that, when connected one after another, makes up the polymer chain. It is shown in square brackets in structural and displayed formulae.

front: How does the repeat unit of a poly(alkene) differ from its monomer?
back: The repeat unit is identical to the monomer except that the **C=C double bond** is replaced by a **C-C single bond**. The repeat unit shown in brackets in a displayed formula is not the monomer itself.

front:
**True or False?**

Poly(chloroethene), also known as PVC, is made by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene monomers.
back:
**True.**

Chloroethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl) undergoes addition polymerisation. The C=C bond opens and the monomers link to form poly(chloroethene), commonly called PVC.

front: Poly(ethene) is formed by the addition polymerisation of **..........**. The repeat unit has a **.......** bond between the two carbon atoms instead of a double bond.
back: Poly(ethene) is formed by the addition polymerisation of **ethene**. The repeat unit has a **single** bond between the two carbon atoms instead of a double bond.

front: How can you identify the monomer from a displayed formula of an addition polymer?
back: Locate the **repeat unit** shown inside square brackets. The monomer is the same as the repeat unit, but with the **C-C single bond** replaced by a **C=C double bond**.

front: Define **non-biodegradable**.
back: A **non-biodegradable** material is one that cannot be broken down by microorganisms. Poly(alkenes) are non-biodegradable and can take hundreds of years to decompose in landfill.

front: Why are poly(alkenes) described as resistant to chemical attack?
back: Poly(alkenes) are very large **alkane-like molecules**. They are **unreactive** and do not undergo chemical reactions, making them **resistant to chemical attack** by most reagents.

front:
**True or False?**

Burning poly(alkenes) is an environmentally safe method of disposal because they combust completely to give only carbon dioxide and water.
back:
**False.**

Burning poly(alkenes) produces harmful combustion products that pollute the environment. Complete combustion to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O is not always achieved, and toxic gases can be released.

front: Poly(alkenes) are **..........**-biodegradable and can take up to **.......** of years to decompose when disposed of in **..........** sites.
back: Poly(alkenes) are **non**-biodegradable and can take up to **hundreds** of years to decompose when disposed of in **landfill** sites.

front: Give three reasons why the disposal of poly(alkenes) is a major environmental challenge.
back:
1. They are **unreactive** and resistant to chemical attack.
2. They are **non-biodegradable**, persisting in landfill for hundreds of years.
3. Burning them produces **harmful combustion products** that pollute the environment.

front:
**True or False?**

Poly(alkenes) are non-biodegradable because they are unreactive large alkane-like molecules.
back:
**True.**

The unreactivity of poly(alkenes) means microorganisms cannot break them down. This is the root cause of their non-biodegradability and long persistence in landfill.

front: Define **landfill**.
back: **Landfill** is a method of waste disposal in which materials are buried underground. Non-biodegradable poly(alkenes) persist for hundreds of years in landfill, causing long-term environmental pollution.

front: Dumping poly(alkenes) in landfill causes long-term **..........**. Burning them releases **.......** combustion products into the atmosphere.
back: Dumping poly(alkenes) in landfill causes long-term **pollution**. Burning them releases **harmful** combustion products into the atmosphere.

front: What chemical property of poly(alkenes) makes them useful as plastics but also problematic for disposal?
back: Their **unreactivity** (resistance to chemical attack) makes them durable and useful as plastics. However, the same property means they are **non-biodegradable** and persist in the environment for very long periods.

front: What reagent is used to test for alkenes, and what is the positive result?
back: Bromine water is used. A positive result is the **decolourisation** of the bromine water from **orange to colourless**, indicating the presence of a **C=C double bond**.

front: Define **nucleophilic substitution**.
back: A **nucleophilic substitution** is an organic reaction mechanism in which a nucleophile attacks a carbon atom carrying a partial positive charge, replacing an atom or group carrying a partial negative charge.

front:
**True or False?**

Tollens' reagent produces a red precipitate with aldehydes.
back:
**False.**

Tollens' reagent produces a silver mirror with aldehydes. A red/orange precipitate is produced by Fehling's solution, not Tollens' reagent.

front: Acidified potassium dichromate oxidises primary alcohols first to **..........**  and then to **..........**, with the solution changing colour from **.......** to green.
back: Acidified potassium dichromate oxidises primary alcohols first to **aldehydes** and then to **carboxylic acids**, with the solution changing colour from **orange** to green.

front: How do you distinguish between an aldehyde and a ketone using Fehling's solution?
back: Fehling's solution gives a **positive result** (blue to red/orange precipitate) with **aldehydes** only. **Ketones** do not react with Fehling's solution. Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, so this reagent cannot distinguish them.

front:
**True or False?**

LiAlH<sub>4</sub> can reduce carboxylic acids to primary alcohols, whereas NaBH<sub>4</sub> cannot.
back:
**True.**

LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a stronger reducing agent and reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols (via an aldehyde intermediate). NaBH<sub>4</sub> cannot reduce carboxylic acids.

front: Define **condensation reaction**.
back: A **condensation reaction** is a reaction in which two organic molecules join together and in the process eliminate a small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride.

front: Amines are produced by heating halogenoalkanes under pressure with **.......** dissolved in **..........** solvent.
back: Amines are produced by heating halogenoalkanes under pressure with **NH**<sub>**3**</sub> dissolved in **ethanol** solvent.

front: What colour change is observed when acidified potassium permanganate reacts with an alkene, and what organic product is formed?
back: The purple KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution turns **colourless**. Acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> causes **oxidative cleavage** of the C=C double bond, producing **carboxylic acids** (from CH<sub>2</sub>= or CH= groups) or **ketones** (from C= groups with no attached hydrogen).

front: What is a multi-step synthetic route in organic chemistry?
back: A multi-step synthetic route is a **sequence of reactions** used to convert a starting material into a target organic molecule, passing through one or more **intermediate** compounds.

front: Define **intermediate**.
back: An **intermediate** is a compound formed during a multi-step synthesis that is then converted into the final product in a subsequent reaction step.

front:
**True or False?**

To convert propan-1-ol into propanoic acid in one step, you heat it with acidified potassium dichromate under reflux.
back:
**True.**

Heating a primary alcohol under reflux with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> oxidises it fully to the carboxylic acid (rather than stopping at the aldehyde, which requires distillation).

front: To make an ester from a primary alcohol in two steps: first **.......** the alcohol to a carboxylic acid, then react it with an alcohol using hot, concentrated **.......** as catalyst.
back: To make an ester from a primary alcohol in two steps: first **oxidise** the alcohol to a carboxylic acid, then react it with an alcohol using hot, concentrated **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> as catalyst.

front: How would you convert propanal into 2-hydroxybutanoic acid using two further reaction steps?
back:
Step 1: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to propanal to form a **hydroxynitrile**.

Step 2: Hydrolysis of the nitrile group using dilute acid (or dilute alkali followed by acidification) to give the **2-hydroxy carboxylic acid**.

front:
**True or False?**

A sodium carboxylate salt can be made by reacting a carboxylic acid with sodium carbonate.
back:
**True.**

Carboxylic acids react with carbonates (including Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) to produce the sodium carboxylate salt, water and CO<sub>2</sub> gas. This is a straightforward acid-base reaction.

front: When devising a multi-step route, you must know which **.......** group each starting material contains and which **.......** each functional group can undergo.
back: When devising a multi-step route, you must know which **functional** group each starting material contains and which **reactions** each functional group can undergo.

front: Outline how ethyl propanoate can be made from propan-1-ol in two steps.
back:
Step 1: Oxidise propan-1-ol to **propanoic acid** using acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> under reflux.

Step 2: React propanoic acid with ethanol in the presence of hot, concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (condensation/esterification) to give **ethyl propanoate** and water.

front: Define **synthetic route**.
back: A **synthetic route** is a planned sequence of chemical reactions that converts a given starting material into a desired target molecule, specifying reagents and conditions for each step.

front: What reagent converts a halogenoalkane into a nitrile, and what is the mechanism?
back: **Ethanolic KCN** (potassium cyanide in ethanol) converts a halogenoalkane into a nitrile by **nucleophilic substitution**. The CN<sup>-</sup> ion acts as the **nucleophile**, replacing the halogen atom.

front: Define **hydroxynitrile**.
back: A **hydroxynitrile** is an organic compound containing both a hydroxyl (OH) group and a nitrile (CN) group. It is formed by nucleophilic addition of HCN (or NaCN) to a carbonyl compound such as an aldehyde.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrolysis of a nitrile with dilute aqueous sulfuric acid under reflux produces a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.
back:
**True.**

Refluxing a nitrile with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) causes hydrolysis of the CN group to give a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt as products.

front: To synthesise hexanoic acid from 1-chloropentane: step 1 — react with **.......** in ethanol to form a nitrile; step 2 — hydrolyse the nitrile with **.......** under reflux.
back: To synthesise hexanoic acid from 1-chloropentane: step 1 — react with **KCN** in ethanol to form a nitrile; step 2 — hydrolyse the nitrile with **dilute H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> under reflux.

front: Why does adding KCN to a halogenoalkane increase the carbon chain length by one?
back: The CN<sup>-</sup> nucleophile adds **one carbon atom** (as part of the CN group) when it replaces the halogen. After hydrolysis of the nitrile to a **carboxylic acid**, the product has one more carbon atom than the original halogenoalkane.

front:
**True or False?**

Nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde produces a hydroxynitrile with the same number of carbon atoms as the aldehyde.
back:
**False.**

Nucleophilic addition of HCN increases the carbon chain by one. The CN group adds across the C=O bond, so the hydroxynitrile has one more carbon than the original aldehyde.

front: In a two-step synthesis of a 2-hydroxy carboxylic acid from an aldehyde: step 1 is nucleophilic addition of **.......** to form a **..........**, and step 2 is **.......** with dilute acid.
back: In a two-step synthesis of a 2-hydroxy carboxylic acid from an aldehyde: step 1 is nucleophilic addition of **HCN** to form a **hydroxynitrile**, and step 2 is **hydrolysis** with dilute acid.

front: When analysing an unfamiliar synthetic route, what is the first step you should take?
back: Identify the **functional groups** present in the starting material and product. Then match the transformation to a known **reaction type** (e.g. oxidation, nucleophilic substitution, hydrolysis) to select appropriate reagents and conditions.

front: Define **nitrile hydrolysis**.
back: **Nitrile hydrolysis** is the reaction of a nitrile (CN group) with dilute aqueous acid or alkali under reflux to produce a carboxylic acid (and an ammonium salt when using acid).

front: Define **fingerprint region**.
back: A **fingerprint region** is the area of an IR spectrum below 1500 cm<sup>-1</sup>. It contains many complex absorption peaks unique to each compound and is used to identify a specific molecule by comparison with reference spectra.

front: What is the characteristic IR absorption range for a C=O bond in a carboxylic acid (carboxyl group)?
back: The C=O bond in a carboxyl group absorbs in the range **1670-1740 cm**<sup>**-1**</sup>. This appears as a strong, sharp peak. The carboxylic acid also shows a **broad O-H peak** at 2500-3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

front:
**True or False?**

The O-H absorption in alcohols appears as a broad peak due to hydrogen bonding.
back:
**True.**

Hydrogen bonding in alcohols causes the O-H bond to vibrate over a range of frequencies, producing a broad absorption peak in the region 3200-3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

front: In IR spectroscopy, absorbed radiation is expressed as **.........** (units: **........**), which are the reciprocal of wavelength.
back: In IR spectroscopy, absorbed radiation is expressed as **wavenumbers** (units: **cm**<sup>**-1**</sup>), which are the reciprocal of wavelength.

front: How can IR spectroscopy be used to distinguish between propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol?
back: Both isomers have the same functional groups and show similar O-H and C-O absorptions above 1500 cm<sup>-1</sup>. They are distinguished by comparing their **fingerprint regions** (below 1500 cm<sup>-1</sup>) with **reference spectra** from a database.

front:
**True or False?**

A strong, sharp absorption at around 1710 cm<sup>-1</sup> in an IR spectrum indicates the presence of a carbonyl (C=O) group in a ketone.
back:
**True.**

Ketone C=O groups absorb strongly and sharply in the range 1680-1750 cm<sup>-1</sup>. A sharp peak around 1710 cm<sup>-1</sup> without a broad O-H absorption confirms a ketone rather than an alcohol.

front: Define **wavenumber**.
back: A **wavenumber** is the number of wave cycles per centimetre, expressed in cm<sup>-1</sup>. It is the reciprocal of wavelength and is used to describe the position of absorption peaks in an IR spectrum.

front: A C≡N nitrile bond absorbs in the range **.........** cm<sup>-1</sup>, while an N-H bond in an amine or amide absorbs in the range **.........** cm<sup>-1</sup>.
back: A C≡N nitrile bond absorbs in the range **2200-2250** cm<sup>-1</sup>, while an N-H bond in an amine or amide absorbs in the range **3300-3500** cm<sup>-1</sup>.

front: Why is IR spectroscopy often used alongside mass spectrometry when identifying an unknown organic compound?
back: Some IR absorption bands overlap, making it impossible to assign all peaks to specific bonds with certainty. Mass spectrometry provides **complementary information** (**molecular mass** and **fragmentation pattern**) that helps confirm the identity of the compound.

front: Define **molecular ion**.
back: A **molecular ion** (M<sup>+</sup>•) is formed when a molecule loses one electron during electron bombardment in mass spectrometry, producing a positively charged species with one unpaired electron.

front: What is the m/e ratio, and how is it used to separate ions in a mass spectrometer?
back: The m/e ratio is the **mass (m)** of an ion divided by its **charge (e)**. Ions are separated by deflection in a magnetic field: ions with a smaller m/e ratio are **deflected more** and detected first.

front:
**True or False?**

The base peak in a mass spectrum corresponds to the most abundant ion fragment.
back:
**True.**

The base peak is the tallest peak in the mass spectrum. It represents the most abundant (most stable) ion fragment produced during electron bombardment and fragmentation.

front: In mass spectrometry, molecules are bombarded with **.......** electrons, causing them to lose an electron and form a positively charged **..........**.
back: In mass spectrometry, molecules are bombarded with **high-energy** electrons, causing them to lose an electron and form a positively charged **molecular ion**.

front: An ion <sup>54</sup>Fe<sup>2+</sup> is detected in a mass spectrometer. What is its m/e value?
back: m/e = 54 ÷ 2 = **27**. Ions with a smaller m/e value are **deflected more** by the magnetic field, so <sup>54</sup>Fe<sup>2+</sup> is deflected more than a heavier or less charged ion with a larger m/e value.

front:
**True or False?**

Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
back:
**True.**

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number (and electron number) but different mass numbers due to differing neutron counts. For example, Cl-35 and Cl-37 are isotopes of chlorine.

front: Define **relative abundance**.
back: **Relative abundance** is the proportion of a particular isotope in a naturally occurring mixture of isotopes of an element, usually expressed as a percentage. Peak heights in a mass spectrum show the relative abundance of each isotope.

front: Chlorine has two naturally occurring isotopes: Cl-35 with a relative abundance of **.......%** and Cl-37 with a relative abundance of **.......%**.
back: Chlorine has two naturally occurring isotopes: Cl-35 with a relative abundance of **75%** and Cl-37 with a relative abundance of **25%**.

front: Why do only positively charged fragment ions reach the detector in a mass spectrometer?
back: The fragments are accelerated by an electric field and then deflected by a magnetic field. Only **positively charged ions** respond to these fields and are directed to the detector. **Neutral molecules and radicals** are not deflected and do not reach the detector.

front: **relative atomic mass**
back: **Relative atomic mass** (*A*<sub>r</sub>) is the weighted average mass of the isotopes of an element, taking into account their relative abundances, expressed relative to 1/12 the mass of carbon-12.

front: State the formula used to calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from isotope data.
back:
*A*<sub>r</sub> = [(relative abundance<sub>1</sub> × mass<sub>1</sub>) + (relative abundance<sub>2</sub> × mass<sub>2</sub>) + ...] ÷ 100

where **relative abundances** are expressed as **percentages**.

front:
**True or False?**

Isotopes of the same element have different numbers of protons.
back:
**False.**

Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons (and electrons) but different numbers of neutrons, giving them different mass numbers.

front: Boron has two isotopes: <sup>10</sup>B (19.9%) and <sup>11</sup>B (80.1%). The relative atomic mass of boron = [(19.9 × **......**) + (80.1 × **......**)] ÷ 100 = **......**.
back: Boron has two isotopes: <sup>10</sup>B (19.9%) and <sup>11</sup>B (80.1%). The relative atomic mass of boron = [(19.9 × **10**) + (80.1 × **11**)] ÷ 100 = **10.80**.

front: How can the relative abundance of isotopes be determined experimentally?
back: By **mass spectrometry**. The heights of the peaks in the mass spectrum correspond to the proportion of each isotope present in the sample, giving their **relative abundances**.

front:
**True or False?**

The relative atomic mass of an element is always equal to the mass number of its most abundant isotope.
back:
**False.**

The relative atomic mass is a weighted average of all isotope masses according to their relative abundances. It is close to the most abundant isotope's mass but is not necessarily equal to it.

front: **isotope**
back: An **isotope** is an atom of the same element as another atom but with a different mass number, due to a different number of neutrons. Isotopes have the same proton number and chemical properties.

front: Why does relative atomic mass appear as a decimal rather than a whole number for most elements?
back: Because relative atomic mass is a **weighted average** of the masses of all naturally occurring isotopes of the element. The weighting reflects the **relative abundance** of each isotope, which rarely produces a whole number result.

front: Define **molecular ion peak**.
back: A **molecular ion peak** is the peak with the highest m/e value in a mass spectrum (ignoring M+1 and M+2 peaks). It corresponds to the intact molecule that has lost one electron and gives the relative molecular mass of the compound.

front: What information about a compound can be obtained from the molecular ion peak in a mass spectrum?
back: The molecular ion peak gives the **relative molecular mass** of the compound. The m/e value of the M<sup>+</sup> peak equals the molecular mass because the ion carries a **single positive charge**.

front:
**True or False?**

A bromine-containing compound shows two molecular ion peaks of approximately equal height, separated by 2 mass units.
back:
**True.**

Bromine has two naturally occurring isotopes, <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br, with approximately equal abundance (50:50). This produces two M<sup>+</sup> peaks of equal height at m/e values 2 apart.

front: In the mass spectrum of alkanes, the fragment C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub><sup>+</sup> appears at m/e = **.......** and the fragment C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub><sup>+</sup> appears at m/e = **.......**.
back: In the mass spectrum of alkanes, the fragment C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub><sup>+</sup> appears at m/e = **29** and the fragment C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub><sup>+</sup> appears at m/e = **43**.

front: Why do alcohols often show a peak 18 units below the molecular ion peak in their mass spectrum?
back: Alcohols readily lose a water molecule (M = 18) during fragmentation. This produces a **[M-18]**<sup>**+**</sup>** peak** corresponding to the alkene cation formed after loss of **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**.

front:
**True or False?**

Fragmentation patterns can distinguish between compounds with the same molecular mass.
back:
**True.**

Different structural isomers can have the same molecular mass but produce different fragmentation patterns. Comparing the m/e values and relative intensities of fragment peaks allows the structure of the compound to be determined.

front: Define **base peak**.
back: A **base peak** is the most intense (tallest) peak in a mass spectrum. It corresponds to the most stable (most abundant) fragment ion produced during electron bombardment.

front: In the mass spectrum of propan-1-ol, loss of a water molecule produces a peak at m/e = **.......**, and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup> fragment appears at m/e = **.......**.
back: In the mass spectrum of propan-1-ol, loss of a water molecule produces a peak at m/e = **42**, and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup> fragment appears at m/e = **31**.

front: How does the m/e value of the molecular ion peak compare to the molecular mass of the compound? Explain why.
back: The m/e value of the molecular ion peak equals the **relative molecular mass**. This is because the molecular ion carries a **single positive charge** (one electron removed), so m/e = M/1 = M.

front: Define **M+1 peak**.
back: An **M+1 peak** is a small peak one mass unit above the molecular ion peak in a mass spectrum. It arises from molecules containing a <sup>13</sup>C atom instead of <sup>12</sup>C. Its size relative to M<sup>+</sup> can be used to calculate the number of carbon atoms.

front: State the formula used to calculate the number of carbon atoms from the M+1 peak.
back:
**n** = (100 × abundance of [M+1]) ÷ (1.1 × abundance of M<sup>+</sup>)

where **n** is the **number of carbon atoms** and abundances are relative (e.g. from peak heights).

front:
**True or False?**

A compound with more carbon atoms will have a larger M+1 peak relative to the M<sup>+</sup> peak.
back:
**True.**

Each carbon atom has a ~1.1% chance of being <sup>13</sup>C. The more carbon atoms in the molecule, the greater the probability that one of them is <sup>13</sup>C, so the M+1 peak is proportionally taller.

front: Carbon-13 makes up approximately **.......%** of all carbon atoms. The ratio of <sup>13</sup>C to <sup>12</sup>C is approximately **.......**.
back: Carbon-13 makes up approximately **1.1%** of all carbon atoms. The ratio of <sup>13</sup>C to <sup>12</sup>C is approximately **1:99**.

front: A compound has an M<sup>+</sup> peak with relative abundance 85 and an [M+1] peak with relative abundance 3. How many carbon atoms are present?
back:
n = (100 × 3) ÷ (1.1 × 85) = 300 ÷ 93.5 = **3.21**

There are **3 carbon atoms** in the compound.

front:
**True or False?**

A compound containing one chlorine atom shows M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2] peaks in a ratio of 3:1.
back:
**True.**

Chlorine has two isotopes: <sup>35</sup>Cl (75% natural abundance) and <sup>37</sup>Cl (25%). A molecule containing one Cl atom therefore shows M<sup>+</sup> (due to <sup>35</sup>Cl) and [M+2] (due to <sup>37</sup>Cl) peaks in a 3:1 ratio.

front: Define **M+2 peak**.
back: An **M+2 peak** is a peak two mass units above the molecular ion peak. It arises from the presence of heavier halogen isotopes (<sup>37</sup>Cl or <sup>81</sup>Br) in the molecule and indicates the presence of chlorine or bromine.

front: A compound with one bromine atom shows M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2] peaks in a ratio of **.......** because <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br have **.......** relative abundances.
back: A compound with one bromine atom shows M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2] peaks in a ratio of **1:1** because <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br have **equal** relative abundances.

front: What pattern of M<sup>+</sup>, [M+2] and [M+4] peaks is observed for a compound containing two bromine atoms, and in what ratio?
back: Three peaks are observed: M<sup>+</sup> (<sup>79</sup>Br + <sup>79</sup>Br), [M+2] (<sup>79</sup>Br + <sup>81</sup>Br) and [M+4] (<sup>81</sup>Br + <sup>81</sup>Br), in a ratio of **1:2:1**.

front: Define **lattice energy**.
back: **Lattice energy** is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.

front:
**True or False?**

Lattice energy is always exothermic.
back:
**True.**

Forming an ionic lattice from gaseous ions always releases energy due to the strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.

front: Write the equation that represents the lattice energy of magnesium chloride.
back: Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s)

front: Define **enthalpy change of atomisation**.
back: **Enthalpy change of atomisation** is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms is formed from its element under standard conditions.

front:
**True or False?**

The enthalpy change of atomisation is always endothermic.
back:
**True.**

Energy is always required to break bonds between atoms in an element to form gaseous atoms, so Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> is always positive.

front: Why can lattice energy not be determined directly by a single experiment?
back: Gaseous ions cannot be brought together in a controlled single-step experiment, so multiple experimental values and an energy cycle (**Born-Haber cycle**) must be used instead.

front:
The enthalpy change of atomisation for sodium is represented by the equation:

Na (**..........** ) → Na (**..........** )
back:
The enthalpy change of atomisation for sodium is represented by the equation:

Na (**s**) → Na (**g**)

front: What does a very large negative value of lattice energy indicate about an ionic compound?
back: It indicates that the ionic compound is much more stable than its gaseous ions, due to **strong electrostatic forces of attraction** between the oppositely charged ions in the solid lattice.

front:
**True or False?**

A more exothermic lattice energy indicates weaker ionic bonds within the lattice.
back:
**False.**

A more exothermic (more negative) lattice energy indicates stronger ionic bonds within the lattice.

front: Define **first electron affinity**.
back: **First electron affinity** (EA<sub>1</sub>) is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous ions each with a single negative charge under standard conditions.

front:
**True or False?**

The second electron affinity of an element is always exothermic.
back:
**False.**

The second electron affinity is endothermic because the incoming electron must overcome repulsion from an already negatively charged ion. Energy is absorbed and the value is positive.

front: Write the equation that represents the first electron affinity of chlorine.
back: Cl (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g)

front: Going down Group 17, the first electron affinity generally becomes **..........**  exothermic because there are more **..........**  shells increasing **..........**.
back: Going down Group 17, the first electron affinity generally becomes **less** exothermic because there are more **electron** shells increasing **shielding**.

front: Why is fluorine's first electron affinity less exothermic than chlorine's, despite fluorine having a higher nuclear charge?
back: Fluorine has a very small **atomic radius**, causing high **electron density** around the nucleus. This leads to increased repulsion between the incoming electron and existing electrons, reducing the overall attraction and making EA<sub>1</sub> less exothermic.

front:
**True or False?**

Electron affinities of non-metals become more exothermic across a period, reaching a maximum at Group 17.
back:
**True.**

Increasing nuclear charge across a period strengthens attraction for the incoming electron, making electron affinity more exothermic up to Group 17.

front: State the three factors that affect the electron affinity of an element.
back:
1. **Nuclear charge**: higher nuclear charge makes EA more exothermic.
2. **Atomic radius**: larger radius makes EA less exothermic.
3. **Shielding**: more inner shells weaken nuclear attraction, making EA less exothermic.

front:
The second electron affinity is represented by:

X<sup>-</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → X**<sup>..........</sup>** (g)

and is **..........**.
back:
The second electron affinity is represented by:

X<sup>-</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → X**<sup>2-</sup>** (g)

and is **endothermic**.

front: Which element in Group 17 has the most exothermic first electron affinity, and what is its value?
back: **Chlorine** has the most exothermic first electron affinity in Group 17, with a value of **-345 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

front: Define **Born-Haber cycle**.
back: A **Born-Haber cycle** is a specific application of Hess's law for ionic compounds, used to calculate lattice enthalpy indirectly from other measurable enthalpy changes.

front: What is the basic principle of drawing a Born-Haber cycle diagram?
back: Energy increases going up the diagram. **Endothermic** steps are shown with arrows pointing upwards and **exothermic** steps with arrows pointing downwards.

front:
**True or False?**

In a Born-Haber cycle, the enthalpy of atomisation step involves breaking bonds and is shown with a downward arrow.
back:
**False.**

Atomisation is endothermic (bond breaking), so it is shown with an upward arrow in the Born-Haber cycle.

front: List the steps required to construct a Born-Haber cycle for potassium chloride, KCl.
back:
1. **Atomisation** of K (s) → K (g)
2. First **ionisation energy** of K (g) → K<sup>+</sup> (g)
3. **Atomisation** of ½Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → Cl (g)
4. First **electron affinity** of Cl (g) → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g)
5. **Enthalpy of formation** of KCl (s)
6. Apply **Hess's law** to find **lattice energy**

front: In a Born-Haber cycle for NaCl, the equation Na (g) → Na<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> represents the **..........**  energy of sodium, which is an **..........**  process.
back: In a Born-Haber cycle for NaCl, the equation Na (g) → Na<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> represents the **ionisation** energy of sodium, which is an **endothermic** process.

front:
**True or False?**

A Born-Haber cycle can only be used to calculate lattice energy.
back:
**False.**

A Born-Haber cycle can be used to calculate any unknown enthalpy change in the cycle, such as enthalpy of formation, electron affinity or ionisation energy, as long as all other values are known.

front: For MgO, why are two ionisation energies and two electron affinities needed in the Born-Haber cycle?
back: Mg forms a **2+** ion, requiring removal of two electrons (**IE**<sub>**1**</sub> and **IE**<sub>**2**</sub>). Oxygen forms a **2-** ion, requiring addition of two electrons (**EA**<sub>**1**</sub> and **EA**<sub>**2**</sub>).

front: The enthalpy change for the direct route in a Born-Haber cycle is the enthalpy of **..........**  and this must equal the **..........**  of all steps in the indirect route.
back: The enthalpy change for the direct route in a Born-Haber cycle is the enthalpy of **formation** and this must equal the **sum** of all steps in the indirect route.

front: Write the equation representing the enthalpy of formation used in the Born-Haber cycle for sodium chloride.
back: Na (s) + ½Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → NaCl (s)       Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -411 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

front: State the equation used to calculate lattice energy from a Born-Haber cycle.
back:
Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> - Δ*H*<sub>1</sub><sup>θ</sup>

where Δ*H*<sub>1</sub><sup>θ</sup> is the sum of all enthalpy changes needed to convert elements in their **standard states** to **gaseous ions**.

front:
**True or False?**

When calculating the lattice energy of MgCl<sub>2</sub>, the electron affinity of chlorine must be doubled.
back:
**True.**

MgCl<sub>2</sub> contains two moles of Cl<sup>-</sup> ions, so two moles of electrons are added to two moles of chlorine atoms. The electron affinity value must be doubled to account for this.

front:
To calculate Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> for KCl:

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> - [(Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> K) + (Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> Cl) + (**..........**) + (**..........** )]
back:
To calculate Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> for KCl:

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> - [(Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> K) + (Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> Cl) + (**IE**<sub>**1**</sub>** K**) + (**EA**<sub>**1**</sub>** Cl**)]

front:
Using the data below, calculate Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> of KCl.

Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> K = +90, Δ*H*<sub>at</sub><sup>θ</sup> Cl = +122, IE<sub>1</sub> K = +418, EA<sub>1</sub> Cl = -349, Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> KCl = -437 (all kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>)

**True or False?**

In a Born-Haber cycle calculation, the direct route always corresponds to the lattice energy.
back:
**False.**

The direct route is the enthalpy change of formation. The lattice energy is part of the indirect route. The stage being calculated is always the direct route.

front: What additional enthalpy terms are needed for MgO compared to KCl in a Born-Haber cycle calculation?
back: MgO requires **IE**<sub>**2**</sub> (second ionisation energy of Mg) and **EA**<sub>**2**</sub> (second electron affinity of O), because Mg forms Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O forms O<sup>2-</sup>.

front:
The simplified Born-Haber equation is:

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>1</sub><sup>θ</sup> + **..........**

Rearranging to find lattice energy:

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = **..........**  - Δ*H*<sub>1</sub><sup>θ</sup>
back:
The simplified Born-Haber equation is:

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>1</sub><sup>θ</sup> + **Δ*****H***<sub>**latt**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup>

Rearranging to find lattice energy:

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = **Δ*****H***<sub>**f**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup> - Δ*H*<sub>1</sub><sup>θ</sup>

front: What principle allows the lattice energy to be calculated from a Born-Haber cycle?
back: **Hess's law**: the total enthalpy change is **independent of the route taken**, so the sum of enthalpy changes along the indirect route equals the enthalpy change of the direct route.

front:
**True or False?**

Using brackets in Born-Haber cycle calculations is recommended to avoid sign errors.
back:
**True.**

Brackets help keep track of positive and negative values when summing multiple enthalpy terms, reducing the chance of arithmetic sign errors.

front: State the two key factors that affect the magnitude of lattice energy.
back:
1. **Ionic charge**: higher charge makes lattice energy more exothermic.
2. **Ionic radius**: smaller radius makes lattice energy more exothermic.

front:
**True or False?**

As ionic radius increases, lattice energy becomes more exothermic.
back:
**False.**

As ionic radius increases, charge density decreases and ions are further apart, so electrostatic attraction is weaker and the lattice energy becomes less exothermic.

front: Both CsF and KF contain F<sup>-</sup> ions. Because Cs<sup>+</sup> is **..........**  than K<sup>+</sup>, the lattice energy of CsF is **..........**  exothermic than that of KF.
back: Both CsF and KF contain F<sup>-</sup> ions. Because Cs<sup>+</sup> is **larger** than K<sup>+</sup>, the lattice energy of CsF is **less** exothermic than that of KF.

front: Explain why the lattice energy of CaO is more exothermic than that of KCl.
back: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> have higher ionic charges than K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>, leading to greater **charge density** and stronger **electrostatic attraction** between ions. Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> are also smaller ions, further increasing the exothermic value.

front:
**True or False?**

Higher ionic charge leads to higher charge density and stronger electrostatic attractions in the lattice.
back:
**True.**

Higher ionic charge means a stronger attraction between oppositely charged ions, so more energy is released when the lattice forms, giving a more exothermic lattice energy.

front: Define **charge density**.
back: **Charge density** is a measure of the ionic charge relative to the ionic volume. It is higher for smaller ions or ions with greater charge.

front: Why does increasing ionic radius cause lattice energy to become less exothermic?
back: Larger ions have lower **charge density**. The charge is spread over a greater volume and the ions are further apart, weakening the **electrostatic attraction** between oppositely charged ions and reducing the energy released.

front: For ions of the same charge, going down a group **..........**  ionic radius and **..........**  charge density, making lattice energy **..........**  exothermic.
back: For ions of the same charge, going down a group **increases** ionic radius and **decreases** charge density, making lattice energy **less** exothermic.

front: Which compound has the more exothermic lattice energy: MgO or CaO? Explain why.
back: MgO has the more exothermic lattice energy. Mg<sup>2+</sup> is smaller than Ca<sup>2+</sup>, so it has a higher **charge density**. This leads to stronger **electrostatic attraction** between Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> and more energy released when the lattice forms.

front: Define **standard enthalpy change of solution**.
back: **Standard enthalpy change of solution** (Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic substance dissolves in sufficient water to form a very dilute solution under standard conditions.

front:
**True or False?**

The enthalpy change of hydration is always exothermic.
back:
**True.**

Hydration enthalpies are always exothermic because energy is released when ion-dipole bonds form between the ions and polar water molecules.

front: Define **standard enthalpy change of hydration**.
back: **Standard enthalpy change of hydration** (Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a specified gaseous ion dissolves in sufficient water to form a very dilute solution under standard conditions.

front: Write an equation to represent the standard enthalpy change of solution of KCl.
back: KCl (s) + aq → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq)

front:
**True or False?**

The enthalpy change of solution can only be exothermic.
back:
**False.**

Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> can be either exothermic or endothermic depending on the relative magnitudes of the lattice energy and the hydration enthalpy.

front: What type of bonds form between water molecules and ions during hydration, and which part of the water molecule is attracted to cations?
back: **Ion-dipole bonds** form during hydration. The δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen atom of water is attracted to positive ions (**cations**). The δ<sup>+</sup> hydrogen atoms are attracted to negative ions (**anions**).

front: When an ionic solid dissolves, the **..........**  of the lattice must be overcome. This energy is compensated for by the **..........**  released during hydration.
back: When an ionic solid dissolves, the **electrostatic attraction** of the lattice must be overcome. This energy is compensated for by the **enthalpy of hydration** released during hydration.

front: Write an equation that represents the standard enthalpy change of hydration of Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions.
back: Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + aq → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

front: The lattice energy of KCl is -711 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. To break the lattice, **..........**  kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> is needed. As Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> of KCl is +26 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, the hydration enthalpy must provide **..........**  kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
back: The lattice energy of KCl is -711 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. To break the lattice, **+711** kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> is needed. As Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> of KCl is +26 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, the hydration enthalpy must provide **-685** kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

front: State the relationship between Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>, Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> and Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> in an energy cycle.
back:
Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>

This can be rearranged to:

Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

In the energy cycle, the direct route from ionic solid to hydrated ions represents the enthalpy change of solution.
back:
**True.**

The direct route (ionic solid → ions in aqueous solution) represents Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>. The indirect route goes via the gaseous ions and involves reverse lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpies.

front:
In the energy cycle for KCl:

Direct route: KCl (s) → KCl (aq) represents **..........**

Indirect route: KCl (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (g) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) → KCl (aq) involves **..........**  and **..........**
back:
In the energy cycle for KCl:

Direct route: KCl (s) → KCl (aq) represents **Δ*****H***<sub>**sol**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup>

Indirect route: KCl (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (g) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) → KCl (aq) involves **-Δ*****H***<sub>**latt**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup> and **Δ*****H***<sub>**hyd**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup>

front: Why is a negative sign placed in front of Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> in the energy cycle equation?
back: Lattice energy (Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup>) refers to lattice formation. In the energy cycle, the lattice is being broken (dissociated), which is the reverse process, so a negative sign is used. This is sometimes referred to as **lattice dissociation enthalpy**.

front:
**True or False?**

The total enthalpy of hydration in the energy cycle is the sum of the hydration enthalpies of each individual ion.
back:
**True.**

Each ion (cation and anion) has its own Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>. The total is found by adding the hydration enthalpies of all ions together.

front: An energy cycle has two routes from ionic lattice to hydrated ions. State what each route represents.
back:
**Route 1 (direct)**: ionic solid → ions in aqueous solution, representing Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>.

**Route 2 (indirect)**: ionic solid → gaseous ions → ions in aqueous solution, representing -Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>.

front: According to Hess's law, the enthalpy change of the **..........**  route equals the enthalpy change of the **..........**  route in an energy cycle.
back: According to Hess's law, the enthalpy change of the **direct** route equals the enthalpy change of the **indirect** route in an energy cycle.

front: Rearrange the energy cycle equation to show how Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> can be calculated.
back:
Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup>

Rearranging: Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> - Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

An energy cycle can only be used to calculate the enthalpy of hydration.
back:
**False.**

An energy cycle can be used to calculate any unknown value among Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>, Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> and Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>, provided the other two are known.

front: State the equation relating Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>, Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> and Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> used in energy cycle calculations.
back: Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>

front: For MgCl<sub>2</sub>, the total Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Mg<sup>2+</sup>] + **..........**  × Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] because there are **..........**  chloride ions.
back: For MgCl<sub>2</sub>, the total Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Mg<sup>2+</sup>] + **2** × Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] because there are **two** chloride ions.

front:
**True or False?**

When calculating Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] in KCl, only the hydration enthalpy of the cation is needed.
back:
**False.**

Both cation and anion hydration enthalpies contribute. The total Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[K<sup>+</sup>] + Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>], so the cation value is used to isolate the anion value.

front:
Using the data below, calculate Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] in KCl.

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup>[KCl] = -711, Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>[KCl] = +26, Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[K<sup>+</sup>] = -322 (all kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>)
back:
Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[K<sup>+</sup>] + Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] = Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>

-322 + Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] = (-711) + (+26) = -685

Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] = -685 + 322 = **-363 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

The equation Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> can be rearranged to find any unknown enthalpy in the cycle.
back:
**True.**

The equation can be rearranged to find Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>, Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> or individual ionic hydration enthalpies, provided the other values are given.

front: In an energy cycle calculation for MgCl<sub>2</sub>, why must Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] be doubled?
back: MgCl<sub>2</sub> contains two Cl<sup>-</sup> ions per formula unit. When 1 mole of MgCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves, 2 moles of Cl<sup>-</sup> ions are hydrated, so the hydration enthalpy of Cl<sup>-</sup> must be multiplied by 2.

front:
To find Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> from an energy cycle:

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> **..........**  Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>
back:
To find Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> from an energy cycle:

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup> **-** Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>

front:
Using these data, calculate Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Mg<sup>2+</sup>].

Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup>[MgCl<sub>2</sub>] = -2592, Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup>[MgCl<sub>2</sub>] = -55, Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] = -363 (all kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>)
back:
Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Mg<sup>2+</sup>] = Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub><sup>θ</sup> + Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub><sup>θ</sup> - 2Δ*H*<sub>hyd</sub><sup>θ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>]

= (-2592) + (-55) - (2 × -363)

= -2647 + 726 = **-1921 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change depends on the route taken between reactants and products.
back:
**False.**

Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change is independent of the route taken. This allows energy cycle calculations to equate the direct and indirect routes.

front: State the two factors that affect the enthalpy change of hydration of an ion.
back:
1. **Ionic radius**: smaller ions have higher charge density and more exothermic hydration enthalpies.
2. **Ionic charge**: higher charge leads to greater charge density and more exothermic hydration enthalpies.

front:
**True or False?**

As ionic radius decreases, the enthalpy change of hydration becomes more exothermic.
back:
**True.**

Smaller ions have higher charge density, forming stronger ion-dipole attractions with water molecules. More energy is released during hydration.

front: Define **ion-dipole attraction**.
back: An **ion-dipole attraction** is the electrostatic force between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar water molecule, responsible for the release of energy during hydration.

front: Explain why the enthalpy of hydration of Mg<sup>2+</sup> is more exothermic than that of Ba<sup>2+</sup>.
back: Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a smaller **ionic radius** than Ba<sup>2+</sup>, giving it a higher **charge density**. This leads to stronger **ion-dipole attractions** with water molecules and more energy released during hydration.

front:
**True or False?**

Higher ionic charge leads to less exothermic hydration enthalpies.
back:
**False.**

Higher ionic charge leads to greater charge density, which strengthens ion-dipole attractions with water molecules and makes hydration enthalpies more exothermic.

front: The enthalpy of hydration of CaO is more exothermic than that of KCl because Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> have **..........**  ionic charges and **..........**  ionic radii than K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>.
back: The enthalpy of hydration of CaO is more exothermic than that of KCl because Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> have **higher** ionic charges and **smaller** ionic radii than K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>.

front: Which ion has the more exothermic enthalpy of hydration: Mg<sup>2+</sup> or Ca<sup>2+</sup>? Give a reason.
back: Mg<sup>2+</sup> has the more exothermic enthalpy of hydration. It has a smaller **ionic radius** than Ca<sup>2+</sup>, giving it a higher **charge density** and stronger **ion-dipole attractions** with water molecules.

front: A smaller ionic radius leads to **..........**  charge density, **..........**  ion-dipole attractions and a **..........**  exothermic enthalpy of hydration.
back: A smaller ionic radius leads to **higher** charge density, **stronger** ion-dipole attractions and a **more** exothermic enthalpy of hydration.

front: Why are hydration enthalpies always exothermic?
back: Energy is released when **ion-dipole bonds** form between the ions and the **polar water molecules** during hydration. Bond formation always releases energy.

front: Define **entropy**.
back: **Entropy** (*S*) is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy in a system. It is a measure of disorder: the greater the disorder, the higher the entropy.

front:
**True or False?**

Gases have greater entropy than liquids, which in turn have greater entropy than solids.
back:
**True.**

The order of entropy is: gas > liquid > solid. Gases are most disordered, solids are most ordered.

front: Explain why the decomposition of CaCO<sub>3</sub> results in an increase in entropy.
back:
CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

A **gaseous** CO<sub>2</sub> molecule is formed from a solid. Gases are far more disordered than solids, so the number of possible arrangements increases and **entropy** increases.

front:
In the Haber process: N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)

Entropy **..........**  because the number of gas molecules **..........**  from 4 to 2.
back:
In the Haber process: N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)

Entropy **decreases** because the number of gas molecules **decreases** from 4 to 2.

front: What happens to the entropy of a substance when it melts, and why?
back: Entropy increases when a substance melts. The regularly arranged **lattice** of particles becomes a more randomly arranged liquid in which particles can rotate and slide over each other, increasing **disorder**.

front:
**True or False?**

Dissolving a solid in a solvent causes a decrease in entropy.
back:
**False.**

Dissolving a solid increases entropy. The particles spread out from the ordered solid lattice into a more disordered solution, increasing the number of possible arrangements.

front: State the order of entropy for the three physical states of matter.
back:
gas > liquid > solid

Gases have the **highest entropy** (most disordered) and solids have the **lowest entropy** (most ordered).

front: When a system becomes more disordered, its **..........** increases.
back: When a system becomes more disordered, its **entropy** increases.

front: Why does entropy decrease during crystallisation of a salt from solution?
back: During **crystallisation**, particles move from a disordered solution into a regular, ordered **solid lattice**. The number of possible arrangements decreases, so entropy decreases.

front: State the equation used to calculate the standard entropy change of a system.
back: Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sub>products</sub><sup>θ</sup> - ΣΔ*S*<sub>reactants</sub><sup>θ</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

All elements have standard molar entropy values of zero.
back:
**False.**

All elements have positive standard molar entropy values. Zero entropy is only reached at absolute zero (0 K).

front:
For the reaction 2Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2MgO (s):

Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (**..........**  × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[MgO]) - (**..........**  × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[Mg] + *S*<sup>θ</sup>[O<sub>2</sub>])
back:
For the reaction 2Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2MgO (s):

Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (**2** × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[MgO]) - (**2** × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[Mg] + *S*<sup>θ</sup>[O<sub>2</sub>])

front:
Calculate Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> for: 2Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2MgO (s)

*S*<sup>θ</sup>[Mg (s)] = 32.60, *S*<sup>θ</sup>[O<sub>2</sub> (g)] = 205.0, *S*<sup>θ</sup>[MgO (s)] = 38.20 (all J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)

**True or False?**

The stoichiometry of a balanced equation must be taken into account when calculating entropy changes.
back:
**True.**

Each entropy value must be multiplied by the corresponding stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced equation before summing.

front: What are the units of standard entropy and standard entropy change?
back: J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

front:
For N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g):

Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (2 × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[NH<sub>3</sub>]) - (*S*<sup>θ</sup>[N<sub>2</sub>] + **..........**  × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[H<sub>2</sub>])
back:
For N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g):

Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (2 × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[NH<sub>3</sub>]) - (*S*<sup>θ</sup>[N<sub>2</sub>] + **3** × *S*<sup>θ</sup>[H<sub>2</sub>])

front: Why is a negative value of Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> expected for the reaction 2Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2MgO (s)?
back: A gas molecule (O<sub>2</sub>) is consumed and no gas is produced. The products are all **solid**, which is more ordered than the reactants. The number of possible arrangements decreases, so Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> is **negative**.

front:
**True or False?**

The state of the compounds must be considered when calculating entropy changes.
back:
**True.**

Entropy values differ significantly between states (gas > liquid > solid), so using the correct state symbol for each compound is essential for an accurate calculation.

front: Define **Gibbs free energy**.
back: **Gibbs free energy** (*G*) is the energy that accounts for both the entropy change and the enthalpy change of a reaction, used to determine reaction feasibility.

front: State the Gibbs equation and give the units of each term.
back:
Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>reaction</sub><sup>θ</sup> - *T*Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup>

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>: kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Δ*H*<sub>reaction</sub><sup>θ</sup>: kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

*T*: K

Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup>: J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> (must be converted to **kJ K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>)

front:
**True or False?**

When using the Gibbs equation, Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> must be converted from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000.
back:
**True.**

The units of Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> are kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, so Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> must be divided by 1000 to ensure consistent units in the calculation.

front:
Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for the reaction: 2NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) at 298 K.

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +135 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>   Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +344 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

The Gibbs equation can be rearranged to find temperature:

*T* = (Δ*H*<sub>reaction</sub><sup>θ</sup> - **..........**) ÷ **..........**
back:
The Gibbs equation can be rearranged to find temperature:

*T* = (Δ*H*<sub>reaction</sub><sup>θ</sup> - **Δ*****G***<sup>**θ**</sup>) ÷ **Δ*****S***<sub>**system**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

The Gibbs free energy change accounts for both enthalpy and entropy changes, making it more reliable than entropy alone for determining feasibility.
back:
**True.**

Using entropy change alone is inaccurate because it ignores the enthalpy contribution. Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> combines both to give a complete picture of feasibility.

front:
Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for: CH<sub>3</sub>OH (l) + HBr (g) → CH<sub>3</sub>Br (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) at 298 K.

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -47 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>   Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -23.0 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
back:
Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -23.0 ÷ 1000 = -0.023 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = -47 - (298 × -0.023)

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **-40.1 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

front: In the Gibbs equation Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>reaction</sub><sup>θ</sup> - *T*Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup>, the symbol *T* represents **..........**  measured in **..........** .
back: In the Gibbs equation Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sub>reaction</sub><sup>θ</sup> - *T*Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup>, the symbol *T* represents **temperature** measured in **kelvin (K)**.

front: Why is it insufficient to use only entropy change to predict whether a reaction is feasible?
back: **Feasibility** depends on both **entropy** and **enthalpy** changes. A reaction with a negative entropy change could still be feasible if it is sufficiently exothermic. The **Gibbs equation** combines both terms to give an accurate prediction.

front: State the condition for a reaction to be feasible in terms of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>.
back: A reaction is feasible when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is **negative** (less than zero). When Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is positive, the reaction is not feasible.

front:
**True or False?**

An exothermic reaction with a positive entropy change is feasible at all temperatures.
back:
**True.**

When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is negative and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive, both terms in Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> - *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are negative at any temperature, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is always negative.

front: Define **feasible reaction**.
back: A **feasible reaction** is one in which Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative, indicating the reaction is thermodynamically likely to occur spontaneously.

front: For an endothermic reaction with a positive Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, at what temperatures is the reaction feasible?
back: At **high temperatures**. The -*T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term becomes sufficiently negative to overcome the positive Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, making Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> **negative** and the reaction feasible.

front:
**True or False?**

An endothermic reaction with a negative entropy change is never feasible.
back:
**True.**

When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is positive and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is negative, both terms in Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> are positive at any temperature. Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is always positive, so the reaction is never feasible.

front: For an exothermic reaction with a negative Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, the reaction is feasible at **..........**  temperatures because the -*T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term does not **..........**  the negative Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>.
back: For an exothermic reaction with a negative Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, the reaction is feasible at **low** temperatures because the -*T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term does not **overcome** the negative Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>.

front:
Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for: 2Ca (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CaO (s) at 298 K.

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = -635.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>   Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -207.0 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is positive and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative only at **..........**  temperatures where *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **..........**  Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>.
back: When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is positive and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative only at **high** temperatures where *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **exceeds** Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>.

front: Explain why an exothermic reaction with a negative entropy change becomes less feasible at high temperatures.
back: At **high temperatures**, the -*T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term becomes large and positive (since Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is negative). This positive term can overcome the negative Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, making Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> positive and the reaction **not feasible**.

front: Define **electrolysis**.
back: An **electrolysis** is the breakdown of a compound into its elements using an electric current passed through a molten ionic compound or concentrated aqueous solution of ions.

front:
**True or False?**

During electrolysis, reduction takes place at the anode and oxidation takes place at the cathode.
back:
**False.**

Oxidation takes place at the anode (anions lose electrons). Reduction takes place at the cathode (cations gain electrons). Remember: RED CATS — REDuction at the CAThode.

front: What determines which cation is discharged at the cathode during electrolysis of an aqueous solution?
back: The cation with the most positive **electrode potential** (*E*<sup>θ</sup>) is discharged, as it is most easily **reduced**. If concentrations are high enough, the more concentrated ion may also be preferentially discharged.

front: During electrolysis, **..........**  ions move to the cathode where they **gain** electrons, and **..........**  ions move to the anode where they **lose** electrons.
back: During electrolysis, **cations** ions move to the cathode where they **gain** electrons, and **anions** ions move to the anode where they **lose** electrons.

front: Give the cathode and anode products when molten aluminium oxide (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) is electrolysed.
back:
**Cathode**: aluminium (Al)

**Anode**: oxygen gas (O<sub>2</sub>)

Al<sup>3+</sup> ions are reduced at the cathode and O<sup>2-</sup> ions are oxidised at the anode.

front:
**True or False?**

When a concentrated aqueous solution of NaCl is electrolysed, chlorine gas forms at the anode rather than oxygen gas.
back:
**True.**

At high Cl<sup>-</sup> concentrations, chloride ions are preferentially discharged at the anode over hydroxide ions, producing Cl<sub>2</sub> gas rather than O<sub>2</sub>.

front: Define **electrolyte**.
back: An **electrolyte** is a molten ionic compound or concentrated aqueous solution of ions that conducts electricity and is broken down during electrolysis.

front: Why is water present in an aqueous electrolyte solution and what ions does it contribute?
back: Water is a **weak electrolyte** that **partially ionises**: H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup>. This adds H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> ions to the solution, which compete with ions from the dissolved salt during electrolysis.

front: Platinum and graphite are used as electrodes in some electrolysis cells because they are **..........**  and do not take part in the reaction.
back: Platinum and graphite are used as electrodes in some electrolysis cells because they are **inert** and do not take part in the reaction.

front: Define **Faraday's constant**.
back: A **Faraday's constant** is the amount of electric charge carried by one mole of electrons or one mole of singly charged ions. Its value is 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>.

front: State the relationship between charge (*Q*), current (*I*) and time (*t*) used in electrolysis calculations.
back:
*Q* = *I* x *t*

where *Q* is in coulombs (C), *I* is in amperes (A) and *t* is in seconds (s).

front:
**True or False?**

One faraday of electricity is required to deposit one mole of magnesium (Mg<sup>2+</sup>) at the cathode.
back:
**False.**

Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Mg requires two moles of electrons, so two faradays (2 × 96 500 C) are needed to deposit one mole of magnesium.

front: The Faraday constant *F* is related to Avogadro's constant *L* and the charge on one electron *e* by: *F* = **..........**
back: The Faraday constant *F* is related to Avogadro's constant *L* and the charge on one electron *e* by: *F* = ***L******* x *******e***

front: Describe how Avogadro's constant (*L*) can be determined experimentally using electrolysis.
back: Copper electrodes are weighed before and after electrolysis of CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq). The **charge passed** and the **mass of copper deposited** are measured. The charge per mole of electrons is calculated and divided by the **charge on one electron** (1.60 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C) to give *L*.

front:
**True or False?**

Four faradays of electricity are needed to form one mole of oxygen gas from the oxidation of OH<sup>-</sup> ions at the anode.
back:
**True.**

4OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) → O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 4e<sup>-</sup>. Four moles of electrons are released per mole of O<sub>2</sub>, so four faradays are required.

front: Define **faraday (unit)**.
back: A **faraday** is the unit of quantity of electricity equal to the charge on one mole of electrons: 1 F = 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>.

front: In an electrolysis experiment to determine Avogadro's constant, why is the mass decrease of the anode often used rather than the mass increase of the cathode?
back: The solid copper deposited at the **cathode** may not adhere properly to the cathode surface, leading to an underestimate in mass gained. The mass lost by the **anode** gives a more reliable measurement.

front: The amount of substance deposited at an electrode during electrolysis is proportional to both the **..........**  and the **..........**  of the constant current passed.
back: The amount of substance deposited at an electrode during electrolysis is proportional to both the **quantity of charge** and the **time** of the constant current passed.

front: Outline the four steps to calculate the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode during electrolysis.
back:
1. Write the **half-equation** at the electrode.
2. Determine the charge (in C) needed to deposit one mole using **Faraday's constant**.
3. Calculate the charge transferred: *Q* = *I* x *t*.
4. Use simple proportion with the **molar mass** to find the mass deposited.

front: The charge *Q* transferred during electrolysis is calculated using *Q* = **..........**  where *I* is in amperes and *t* is in **..........** .
back: The charge *Q* transferred during electrolysis is calculated using *Q* = ***I******* × *******t*** where *I* is in amperes and *t* is in **seconds**.

front:
**True or False?**

To deposit one mole of silver (Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> → Ag) requires 193 000 C of electricity.
back:
**False.**

Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> → Ag involves only one mole of electrons, so only one faraday (96 500 C) is required to deposit one mole of silver.

front: How many coulombs are needed to deposit one mole of magnesium from Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions at the cathode?
back:
Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Mg requires 2 moles of electrons.

Charge = 2 × 96 500 = **193 000 C**

front: Define **electrolysis calculation**.
back: An **electrolysis calculation** is a method that uses the charge passed (*Q* = *I* × *t*), Faraday's constant and the half-equation to find the mass or volume of substance produced or deposited at an electrode.

front:
**True or False?**

At room temperature, one mole of any gas produced at an electrode during electrolysis occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup>.
back:
**True.**

The molar volume of a gas at room temperature is 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. This value is used when calculating volumes of gas liberated at electrodes.

front: A current of 0.50 A flows for 10 minutes through molten CaCl<sub>2</sub>. How many coulombs are transferred?
To produce one mole of O<sub>2</sub> gas at the anode (4OH<sup>-</sup> → O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e<sup>-</sup>), **..........**  C of electricity is required.
back: To produce one mole of O<sub>2</sub> gas at the anode (4OH<sup>-</sup> → O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e<sup>-</sup>), **386 000** C of electricity is required.

front: Why is the time converted to seconds (not minutes) when using *Q* = *I* × *t* in electrolysis calculations?
back: Because current is measured in **amperes** (A = C s<sup>-1</sup>) and the resulting charge *Q* must be in **coulombs** (C). Using minutes would give an incorrect value of *Q* and an incorrect mass or volume.

front: Define **standard electrode potential**.
back: A **standard electrode potential** (*E*<sup>ɔ</sup>) is the voltage produced when a standard half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions (1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, 298 K, 1 atm).

front: State the standard conditions required when measuring electrode potentials.
back:
- Ion concentration: **1.00 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>
- Temperature: **298 K (25 °C)**
- Pressure: **1 atm**

front:
**True or False?**

A more positive standard electrode potential indicates that the species is more easily reduced.
back:
**True.**

A more positive *E*<sup>ɔ</sup> means the equilibrium position lies further to the right, so the species on the left of the half-equation is more readily reduced.

front: Define **standard hydrogen electrode**.
