front: What precipitate forms when NaOH is added dropwise to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>?
back: A **blue precipitate** of [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub>] forms as two water ligands are partially substituted by two hydroxide ligands.

front: When water is added to [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>, the **..........**  ligands displace the chloride ions and the **..........**  solution returns.
back: When water is added to [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>, the **water** ligands displace the chloride ions and the **blue** solution returns.

front: Define **hexaaqua complex**.
back: A **hexaaqua complex** is a transition metal complex in which six water molecules act as ligands, each donating a lone pair to the central metal ion to form an octahedral complex such as [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

front: Define **standard electrode potential**.
back: A **standard electrode potential** (*E*<sup>θ</sup>) is the potential of a half-cell measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions, indicating how readily a species is reduced.

front: How do you calculate the standard cell potential for a redox reaction?
back: *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduction</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidation</sub>. A **positive** value indicates the reaction is feasible.

front:
**True or False?**

A more positive standard electrode potential means a species is more readily oxidised.
back: **False.** A more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> means the species is more readily **reduced** (gains electrons more readily). The more negative the *E*<sup>θ</sup>, the more readily the species is oxidised.

front: Half equations are always written as **..........**  reactions. The species with the more **..........**  *E*<sup>θ</sup> acts as the oxidising agent.
back: Half equations are always written as **reduction** reactions. The species with the more **positive** *E*<sup>θ</sup> acts as the oxidising agent.

front: Given *E*<sup>θ</sup> for Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> = +0.77 V and Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu<sup>+</sup> = +0.15 V, calculate *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for the reaction Fe<sup>3+</sup> + Cu<sup>+</sup> → Fe<sup>2+</sup> + Cu<sup>2+</sup>.
back: *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = (+0.77) − (+0.15) = **+0.62 V**. The positive value confirms the reaction is **feasible**.

front:
**True or False?**

A positive standard cell potential guarantees that a reaction will occur in practice.
back: **False.** A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> indicates **feasibility** but does not guarantee the reaction will occur. A large activation energy barrier may prevent the reaction from proceeding.

front: In the half equation Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>, the **..........**  ion is the oxidising agent and iron undergoes **..........** .
back: In the half equation Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>, the **Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup> ion is the oxidising agent and iron undergoes **reduction**.

front: Define **feasibility of a redox reaction**.
back: **Feasibility of a redox reaction** is whether it is thermodynamically likely to occur, predicted by comparing standard electrode potentials: a positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> value indicates a feasible reaction.

front: In a redox reaction, which half equation is reversed to represent oxidation?
back: The half equation with the **less positive** (or more negative) standard electrode potential is reversed, so the species is **oxidised** rather than reduced.

front: What is the overall equation for the redox reaction between MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> and C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> in acid solution?
back: 5C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) + 16H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 8H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 10CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

front: Define **autocatalyst**.
back: An **autocatalyst** is a product of a reaction that catalyses the same reaction, causing it to accelerate as more product is formed. In the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>/C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> reaction, Mn<sup>2+</sup> acts as the autocatalyst.

front:
**True or False?**

In the reaction of Fe<sup>2+</sup> with MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> in acid, the endpoint is when a permanent pink colour appears.
back: **True.** The purple MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> colour disappears as it reacts with Fe<sup>2+</sup>. The endpoint is when all Fe<sup>2+</sup> has reacted and a trace of permanent **pink** appears, indicating a slight excess of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>.

front: Write the overall equation for the reaction of Fe<sup>2+</sup> with MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> in acid.
back: 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq)

front: In the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/I<sup>-</sup> redox system, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is **..........**  to Cu<sup>+</sup> while I<sup>-</sup> is **..........**  to I<sub>2</sub>.
back: In the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/I<sup>-</sup> redox system, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is **reduced** to Cu<sup>+</sup> while I<sup>-</sup> is **oxidised** to I<sub>2</sub>.

front:
**True or False?**

In the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/I<sup>-</sup> titration, starch is added at the start to indicate the endpoint.
back: **False.** Starch is added when **most of the iodine colour has faded**, not at the start. It turns deep blue/black in the presence of the remaining I<sub>2</sub> and the endpoint is when this colour disappears.

front: In the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/I<sup>-</sup> system, what is the role of sodium thiosulfate in the second reaction?
back: **Sodium thiosulfate** reacts with the iodine produced: I<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) → 2I<sup>-</sup> (aq) + S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq). The moles of thiosulfate are used to calculate the **moles of Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>.

front: In the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>/C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> reaction, the oxidation number of manganese changes from **..........**  to **..........** , so MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is **..........** .
back: In the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>/C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> reaction, the oxidation number of manganese changes from **+7** to **+2**, so MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is **reduced**.

front: Define **redox titration**.
back: A **redox titration** is a titration in which one species is oxidised and another is reduced, used to find the concentration of an unknown species by measuring the volume of a standard solution required to reach the endpoint.

front: Define **degenerate orbitals**.
back: **Degenerate orbitals** are orbitals that are equal in energy. In an isolated transition element ion, all five 3d orbitals are degenerate.

front: What causes the 3d orbitals to split into non-degenerate sets?
back: When **ligands** form dative bonds with the central metal ion, the lone pairs of the ligands repel the d orbital electrons by different amounts depending on orbital orientation, causing the five d orbitals to split into two sets of unequal energy.

front:
**True or False?**

In an octahedral complex, the 3d<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup><sub>-y</sub><sup>2</sup> and 3d<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup> orbitals are at a lower energy than the other three d orbitals.
back: **False.** In an octahedral complex, the 3d<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup><sub>-y</sub><sup>2</sup> and 3d<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup> orbitals are at a **higher** energy because they point along the axes where the ligands approach, causing greater repulsion.

front: In an octahedral complex, the ligands approach along the **..........**,  causing greater repulsion with the **..........**  and 3d<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup> orbitals.
back: In an octahedral complex, the ligands approach along the **x, y and z axes**, causing greater repulsion with the **3d**<sub>**x**</sub><sup>**2**</sup><sub>**-y**</sub><sup>**2**</sup> and 3d<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup> orbitals.

front: Define **non-degenerate orbitals**.
back: **Non-degenerate orbitals** are orbitals that are not equal in energy. In a transition element complex, ligand bonding splits the five 3d orbitals into two sets of non-degenerate orbitals.

front: In a tetrahedral complex, which set of d orbitals is at higher energy after splitting?
back: In a tetrahedral complex, the **3d**<sub>**yz**</sub>**, 3d**<sub>**xz**</sub>** and 3d**<sub>**xy**</sub> orbitals are at higher energy because the ligand bonding pairs align with these orbitals, causing greater repulsion.

front:
**True or False?**

The energy gap between the two sets of non-degenerate d orbitals is labelled ΔE.
back: **True.** The energy difference between the two sets of non-degenerate d orbitals in a complex is called **Δ*E***.

front: An isolated transition element ion has **..........**  degenerate d orbitals. When ligands bind, these split into **..........**  sets of non-degenerate orbitals.
back: An isolated transition element ion has **five** degenerate d orbitals. When ligands bind, these split into **two** sets of non-degenerate orbitals.

front: Why do the 3d<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup><sub>-y</sub><sup>2</sup> and 3d<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup> orbitals experience more repulsion from ligands in an octahedral complex?
back: These two orbitals have lobes pointing **along** the x, y and z axes — the same directions from which the six ligands approach. Their electrons are therefore closer to the bonding electrons of the ligands, causing more repulsion.

front: Define **complementary colour**.
back: A **complementary colour** is the colour observed from a transition element complex — it is made up of the wavelengths of visible light that are **not** absorbed by the complex.

front: Why do transition element complexes appear coloured?
back: Ligands cause the d orbitals to split into non-degenerate sets. Electrons absorb light of a specific frequency (equal to ΔE) and are promoted to a higher energy orbital. The **complementary colour** — the frequencies not absorbed — is what we observe.

front:
**True or False?**

Changing the ligand on a transition metal complex can change the colour of the complex, even if the oxidation state of the metal remains the same.
back: **True.** Different ligands split the d orbitals by different amounts of energy (different ΔE), so a different frequency of light is absorbed, resulting in a different complementary colour.

front: The equation relating energy absorbed to frequency is ΔE = **..........**  × **..........**,  where h is Planck's constant.
back: The equation relating energy absorbed to frequency is ΔE = ***h*** × ***ν***, where h is Planck's constant.

front: What colour change occurs when ammonia ligands replace water ligands in [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>?
back: The complex changes from **light blue** ([Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>) to **dark blue** ([Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>) because the ammonia ligands split the d orbitals by a different ΔE.

front:
**True or False?**

[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is pink and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is brown.
back: **True.** The change from water to ammonia ligands alters ΔE and therefore the frequency of light absorbed, causing the observed colour to change from **pink** to **brown**.

front: Define **electron promotion**.
back: **Electron promotion** is the process in which an electron in a transition metal complex absorbs light energy equal to ΔE and jumps from a lower to a higher non-degenerate d orbital.

front: Why does [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub>] appear pale blue while [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> appears yellow?
back: The chloride ligands split the d orbitals by a **different ΔE** compared to water and hydroxide. This changes the frequency of light absorbed, so the complementary colour observed shifts from pale blue to **yellow**.

front: Copper(II) ions absorb light from the **..........**  end of the spectrum, so the observed colour is **..........**.
back: Copper(II) ions absorb light from the **red** end of the spectrum, so the observed colour is **pale blue (cyan)**.

front: Define **cis-trans isomerism in complexes**.
back: **Cis-trans isomerism in complexes** is a type of stereoisomerism found in square planar and octahedral complexes with two pairs of different ligands. In the cis isomer, identical ligands are adjacent; in the trans isomer, they are opposite each other.

front: Why is cisplatin medically active while transplatin is not?
back: Cisplatin is **polar** because the two electronegative Cl ligands are on the same side, creating a charge imbalance that allows it to bind to DNA. Transplatin is **non-polar** because the ligands are opposite each other, so the charges cancel.

front:
**True or False?**

Octahedral complexes with three identical bidentate ligands can exhibit optical isomerism.
back: **True.** Such complexes have no plane of symmetry and exist as non-superimposable mirror images — the defining feature of **optical isomers**.

front: In a trans isomer of an octahedral complex, the two different ligands are positioned **..........**  each other, making the complex **..........** .
back: In a trans isomer of an octahedral complex, the two different ligands are positioned **opposite** each other, making the complex **non-polar**.

front: What structural feature allows octahedral complexes to display cis-trans isomerism?
back: An octahedral complex displays cis-trans isomerism when it has **two ligands that are different** from the other four. These two different ligands can be either adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).

front:
**True or False?**

Optical isomers of complexes rotate the plane of polarised light in the same direction.
back: **False.** The two optical isomers rotate the plane of polarised light in **opposite** directions. This is their only difference in properties.

front: Define **optical isomers**.
back: **Optical isomers** are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. They have no plane of symmetry and differ only in the direction in which they rotate the plane of polarised light.

front: Why is the cis isomer of [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> polar?
back: In the cis isomer, the two H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are on the same side. The oxygen atoms in water are more electronegative than the nitrogen atoms in NH<sub>3</sub>, creating a partial negative charge on one side and making the complex **polar**.

front: Cisplatin is a **..........**  planar complex with two **..........**  and two **..........**  ligands.
back: Cisplatin is a **square** planar complex with two **Cl**<sup>**-**</sup> and two **NH**<sub>**3**</sub> ligands.

front: Define **stability constant (*****K*****<sub>stab</sub>**).
back: A **stability constant** (*K*<sub>stab</sub>) is the equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion from its constituent central metal ion and ligands in solution. A larger value indicates a more stable complex.

front: Why is the concentration of water not included in the K<sub>stab</sub> expression?
back: Water is present in **excess** as the solvent. Any water produced by the ligand substitution is negligible compared to the water already present, so its concentration is treated as constant and omitted.

front:
**True or False?**

A larger K<sub>stab</sub> value indicates a more stable complex.
back: **True.** The larger the *K*<sub>stab</sub>, the further the equilibrium lies towards the products, meaning the complex formed is more stable.

front: For the reaction [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O, the *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression is: *K*<sub>stab</sub> = **..........** .
back: For the reaction [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O, the *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression is: *K*<sub>stab</sub> = **[[Cu(NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**4**</sub>**(H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O)**<sub>**2**</sub>**]**<sup>**2+**</sup>**] / [[Cu(H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O)**<sub>**6**</sub>**]**<sup>**2+**</sup>**][NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**]**<sup>**4**</sup>.

front: What is meant by stepwise stability constants in ligand substitution?
back: In stepwise substitution, each individual ligand replacement has its own equilibrium constant (K<sub>1</sub>, K<sub>2</sub>, etc.). The **overall stability constant** *K*<sub>stab</sub> summarises all the stepwise constants combined.

front:
**True or False?**

Stability constants are often expressed on a log<sub>10</sub> scale to make comparison easier.
back: **True.** The log<sub>10</sub> scale is used because *K*<sub>stab</sub> values span many orders of magnitude, making them easier to compare.

front: In the K<sub>stab</sub> expression, what does the position of equilibrium tell you if K<sub>stab</sub> is very large?
back: A very large *K*<sub>stab</sub> means the equilibrium lies far to the **right**, with **products** (the complex) strongly favoured over the constituent ions and ligands.

front: When a 0.15 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]<sup>+</sup> reacts with 0.15 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Cl<sup>-</sup> to give 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> at equilibrium, the *K*<sub>stab</sub> = **..........**  dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
back: When a 0.15 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]<sup>+</sup> reacts with 0.15 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Cl<sup>-</sup> to give 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> at equilibrium, the *K*<sub>stab</sub> = **40** dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.

front: Define **competing equilibrium**.
back: A **competing equilibrium** in ligand exchange is the simultaneous existence of multiple substitution equilibria in solution, with the most stable complex (highest *K*<sub>stab</sub>) being preferentially formed.

front: Why does ligand exchange occur in a transition metal complex?
back: Ligand exchange occurs because the incoming ligands form a **more stable** complex, with a **larger *****K***<sub>**stab**</sub>, than the original complex. The equilibrium shifts to favour the more stable product.

front:
**True or False?**

The complex [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> is more stable than [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> based on their stability constants.
back: **False.** The log<sub>10</sub> *K*<sub>stab</sub> of the NH<sub>3</sub> complex (13.1) is greater than that of the Cl<sup>-</sup> complex (5.6), so the **ammonia complex is more stable**.

front: Define **log****<sub>10</sub>**** *****K*****<sub>stab</sub>**.
back: **log**<sub>**10**</sub>** *****K***<sub>**stab**</sub> is the stability constant expressed on a base-10 logarithmic scale, making it easier to compare the relative stabilities of different complexes across a wide range of values.

front: When excess NH<sub>3</sub> is added to [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>, the chloride ligands are replaced by ammonia because the ammonia complex has a **..........**  *K*<sub>stab</sub>, shifting the equilibrium to the **..........** .
back: When excess NH<sub>3</sub> is added to [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>, the chloride ligands are replaced by ammonia because the ammonia complex has a **larger** *K*<sub>stab</sub>, shifting the equilibrium to the **right**.

front: Given that log<sub>10</sub> *K*<sub>stab</sub> for [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>-</sup> = 18.7 and for [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> = 6.2, which complex is more stable?
back: [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>-</sup> is more stable because it has the **larger** log<sub>10</sub> *K*<sub>stab</sub> value (18.7 vs 6.2), meaning its equilibrium lies further to the right with a greater proportion of complex formed.

front:
**True or False?**

A higher K<sub>stab</sub> means the equilibrium lies further to the right, favouring the complex.
back: **True.** A higher *K*<sub>stab</sub> value means the complex is more thermodynamically stable and the equilibrium position lies further towards the products.

front: Three silver complexes have *K*<sub>stab</sub> values: [Ag(S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3-</sup> = 2.9 × 10<sup>13</sup>, [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>-</sup> = 5.3 × 10<sup>18</sup>, [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> = 1.6 × 10<sup>7</sup>. Which has the lowest concentration at equilibrium if all ligands are present equally?
back: [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> has the **lowest concentration** because it has the smallest *K*<sub>stab</sub> value and is the least stable complex.

front: Ligand exchange forms a new complex that is **..........**  than the original. The position of equilibrium shifts to the **..........**.
back: Ligand exchange forms a new complex that is **more stable** than the original. The position of equilibrium shifts to the **right**.

front: Define **stability constant comparison**.
back: **Stability constant comparison** is the use of *K*<sub>stab</sub> values to determine which complex is more stable: the complex with the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> is preferentially formed when ligands compete for the same metal ion.

front: Define **functional group**.
back: A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms in an organic molecule that determines its characteristic chemical and physical properties.

front: Why do arenes prefer substitution reactions over addition reactions?
back: Arenes prefer substitution reactions because the delocalised π electron ring system is extremely stable. Addition reactions would disrupt this **aromatic stabilisation**, whereas substitution reactions maintain the delocalised ring.

front:
**True or False?**

Halogenoarenes are soluble in water due to the halogen atom attached to the ring.
back:
**False.**

Halogenoarenes are insoluble in water. The non-polar hydrocarbon ring means it is not energetically favourable for halogenoarene molecules to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.

front: Amines are basic due to the **..........** on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.
back: Amines are basic due to the **lone pair of electrons** on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.

front: Define **phenol**.
back: A **phenol** is an aromatic compound containing a hydroxyl group (–OH) bonded directly to a benzene ring.

front: Why is the –OH group in phenol more acidic than in alcohols?
back: The oxygen in phenol donates one of its **lone pairs** into the ring's π system, increasing electron density in the ring. This weakens the **O–H bond**, making the hydrogen easier to donate and phenol more acidic than an alcohol.

front:
**True or False?**

Amides are more basic than amines.
back:
**False.**

Amides are less basic than amines because the lone pair on the nitrogen is delocalised into the adjacent C=O group, making it less available to accept a proton.

front: Acyl chlorides are extremely reactive and readily undergo **..........** reactions in which the chlorine atom is replaced by another species.
back: Acyl chlorides are extremely reactive and readily undergo **substitution** reactions in which the chlorine atom is replaced by another species.

front: What structural features define an amino acid?
back: An amino acid contains both an **amine group** (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and a **carboxyl group** (–COOH). Most amino acids have a chiral centre and exhibit optical isomers, except for glycine.

front: Define **skeletal formula**.
back: A **skeletal formula** is a simplified structural representation of an organic molecule that shows the carbon skeleton as a zigzag, with functional groups shown explicitly and hydrogen atoms on carbon omitted.

front: What is the difference between a structural formula and a displayed formula?
back: A **structural formula** shows how atoms are grouped and bonded without showing all individual bonds. A **displayed formula** shows every bond in the molecule explicitly, including all C–H bonds.

front:
**True or False?**

A general formula can be used to represent all members of a homologous series.
back:
**True.**

A general formula gives the simplest algebraic expression for any member of a homologous series. For example, alkanes have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>.

front: In a skeletal formula, carbon atoms are represented by **..........** in a zigzag chain, and hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are **..........** .
back: In a skeletal formula, carbon atoms are represented by **vertices/line ends** in a zigzag chain, and hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are **not shown**.

front: Define **general formula**.
back: A **general formula** is the simplest algebraic expression that describes the molecular formula of any member of a homologous series.

front: Which type of formula shows every atom and bond in a molecule?
back: A displayed formula shows **every atom and every bond** in the molecule, including all C–H bonds.

front:
**True or False?**

A structural formula shows all individual C–H bonds explicitly.
back:
**False.**

A structural formula groups atoms together (e.g. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) without drawing every individual bond. It is the displayed formula that shows all bonds explicitly.

front: The four types of formula used for organic compounds are: general formula, **..........**  , displayed formula and skeletal formula.
back: The four types of formula used for organic compounds are: general formula, **structural formula**, displayed formula and skeletal formula.

front: Why are skeletal formulae particularly useful for complex organic molecules?
back: Skeletal formulae are useful for complex molecules because they omit carbon and hydrogen atoms on the chain, making the structure cleaner and easier to read. **Functional groups and heteroatoms** are still shown explicitly.

front: Define **systematic nomenclature**.
back: A **systematic nomenclature** is a standardised method of naming organic compounds based on the length of the longest carbon chain, the functional group present and the positions of substituents.

front: What is the first step when naming an aliphatic organic compound systematically?
back: Identify the **longest carbon chain** that contains the **principal functional group**. This gives the parent chain name and the base suffix.

front:
**True or False?**

When numbering the carbon chain, the functional group should be given the highest possible locant.
back:
**False.**

The carbon chain should be numbered so that the principal functional group has the **lowest** possible locant.

front: When two or more identical substituents are present, the prefixes **..........**  , tri- or tetra- are added before the substituent name.
back: When two or more identical substituents are present, the prefixes **di-**, tri- or tetra- are added before the substituent name.

front: Define **aromatic compound**.
back: An **aromatic compound** is an organic compound that contains a benzene ring with a conjugated π system of delocalised electrons.

front: How is the naming of aromatic compounds similar to that of aliphatic compounds?
back: Both use the position numbering system to indicate where substituents are located. For aromatic compounds, benzene is the parent name and substituents are numbered to give the **lowest possible locants**.

front:
**True or False?**

Multiple substituents on a benzene ring are listed alphabetically before the parent name.
back:
**True.**

Substituents on a benzene ring (and on aliphatic chains) are listed as prefixes in alphabetical order before the parent chain name.

front: In 2-methylchlorobenzene, the number 2 indicates the position of the **..........** group relative to the **..........** group.
back: In 2-methylchlorobenzene, the number 2 indicates the position of the **methyl** group relative to the **chloro** group.

front: What suffix is used in the name of an amide, and what functional group does it indicate?
back: The suffix **-amide** is used. It indicates the presence of the –CONH<sub>2</sub> group, which contains a carbonyl (C=O) and an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>) group.

front: Define **electrophile**.
back: An **electrophile** is an electron-deficient species that acts as an electron pair acceptor, attracted to regions of high electron density.

front: What is an electrophilic substitution reaction?
back: An electrophilic substitution reaction is one in which an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by an **electron pair acceptor** after an initial attack by that electron-deficient species.

front:
**True or False?**

Benzene undergoes addition reactions rather than substitution reactions when reacting with bromine.
back:
**False.**

Benzene undergoes substitution reactions (electrophilic substitution), not addition reactions. The aromatic stability of the benzene ring is maintained by substitution rather than addition.

front: Define **nucleophilic addition-elimination**.
back: A **nucleophilic addition-elimination** is a reaction type in which a nucleophile adds across a C=O bond (addition), followed by the loss of a small molecule such as HCl (elimination).

front: The hydrolysis of an acyl chloride is a nucleophilic addition-elimination reaction producing a **..........** and **..........** as products.
back: The hydrolysis of an acyl chloride is a nucleophilic addition-elimination reaction producing a **carboxylic acid** and **HCl** as products.

front: Give three examples of nucleophilic addition-elimination reactions of acyl chlorides.
back:
1. Hydrolysis with water to form a **carboxylic acid** and HCl.
2. Reaction with an alcohol to form an **ester** and HCl.
3. Reaction with ammonia or a primary amine to form an **amide** and HCl.

front:
**True or False?**

In the esterification of an acyl chloride with an alcohol, the alcohol adds across the C–Cl bond.
back:
**False.**

The alcohol adds across the C=O bond (the carbonyl). The HCl molecule is then eliminated in the second step.

front: When propanoyl chloride reacts with a primary amine, the nitrogen's **..........** attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming an amide after elimination of **..........** .
back: When propanoyl chloride reacts with a primary amine, the nitrogen's **lone pair** attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming an amide after elimination of **HCl**.

front: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic substitution rather than addition when reacting with bromine?
back: Benzene's delocalised π electron ring system is highly stable (**aromaticity**). Substitution preserves this aromaticity by replacing H with Br. Addition would disrupt the delocalised ring and is energetically unfavourable.

front: Define **conjugated π system**.
back: A **conjugated π system** is a region of alternating single and double bonds in which electrons are delocalised across adjacent p orbitals, spreading electron density over the whole system.

front: What type of hybridisation do the carbon atoms in benzene have, and what does this mean for their bonding?
back: Carbon atoms in benzene are **sp**<sup>**2**</sup>** hybridised**. Each carbon forms three σ bonds using its sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals and has one remaining p orbital that overlaps laterally with neighbouring p orbitals to form the **delocalised π system**.

front:
**True or False?**

All carbon–carbon bond lengths in benzene are equal.
back:
**True.**

Because electrons are delocalised across the ring, all C–C bonds have the same length with both single and double bond character. This equal bond length is evidence for the delocalised ring structure.

front: Benzene is a **..........** molecule with bond angles of **..........** due to sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation of its carbon atoms.
back: Benzene is a **planar** molecule with bond angles of **120°** due to sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation of its carbon atoms.

front: Define **aromatic stabilisation**.
back: An **aromatic stabilisation** is the extra stability gained by a molecule due to the delocalisation of π electrons over a conjugated ring system, making the compound more stable than predicted by a simple alternating double bond model.

front: How does the p orbital overlap in benzene lead to delocalisation of electrons?
back: Each sp<sup>2</sup>-hybridised carbon retains one **p orbital** perpendicular to the ring. These p orbitals on adjacent carbons overlap laterally around the ring, allowing electrons to spread freely across all six carbon atoms rather than being **localised** in fixed double bonds.

front:
**True or False?**

In sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation, the carbon's s orbital mixes with all three of its p orbitals.
back:
**False.**

In sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation, the s orbital mixes with only two of the three p orbitals, forming three sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals. The remaining p orbital is unhybridised and participates in the π system.

front: Aromatic compounds often have pleasant odours. The word 'aromatic' in chemistry refers to compounds containing one or more rings with **..........** π systems.
back: Aromatic compounds often have pleasant odours. The word 'aromatic' in chemistry refers to compounds containing one or more rings with **conjugated** π systems.

front: What evidence supports the delocalised ring structure of benzene?
back: All C–C bonds in benzene are the **same length**, **intermediate** between a C–C single bond and a C=C double bond. If benzene had alternating single and double bonds, two different bond lengths would be observed.

front: Define **chiral centre**.
back: A **chiral centre** is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups of atoms, giving rise to a pair of non-superimposable mirror image molecules (enantiomers).

front: How do the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule differ?
back: Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties but differ in the direction they rotate plane polarised light. One rotates it **clockwise** (+) and the other **anticlockwise** (−). They may also have different biological activities.

front:
**True or False?**

A racemic mixture rotates plane polarised light because one enantiomer is always present in a slightly greater proportion.
back:
**False.**

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both enantiomers. Their opposite rotations cancel out exactly, so the mixture is optically inactive and there is no net rotation of plane polarised light.

front: Define **racemic mixture**.
back: A **racemic mixture** is a mixture containing equal amounts of the two enantiomers of a chiral compound, making it optically inactive.

front: The (+) enantiomer rotates plane polarised light in the **..........** direction, while the (−) enantiomer rotates it **..........** .
back: The (+) enantiomer rotates plane polarised light in the **clockwise** direction, while the (−) enantiomer rotates it **anticlockwise**.

front: Why do enantiomers often have different biological activities?
back: Enzymes are chiral proteins with specific binding sites. Only the enantiomer with the correct shape fits the **active site**. The mirror image enantiomer will not bind as well, giving it a different or absent biological effect.

front:
**True or False?**

Enantiomers are superimposable mirror images of each other.
back:
**False.**

Enantiomers are **non-superimposable** mirror images. They cannot be placed on top of each other and be identical, just as a left hand cannot be superimposed on a right hand.

front: A solution containing 80% of the clockwise-rotating enantiomer and 20% of the anticlockwise-rotating enantiomer is said to be optically **..........** and will rotate light **..........** .
back: A solution containing 80% of the clockwise-rotating enantiomer and 20% of the anticlockwise-rotating enantiomer is said to be optically **active** and will rotate light **clockwise**.

front: How can plane polarised light be used to distinguish between enantiomers?
back: Plane polarised light is passed through a solution of one enantiomer. The direction of rotation of the plane indicates which isomer is present: clockwise rotation identifies the **(+) enantiomer** and anticlockwise rotation identifies the **(−) enantiomer**. A racemic mixture gives no rotation.

front: Define **chiral catalyst**.
back: A **chiral catalyst** is a catalyst that directs a reaction to produce predominantly one enantiomer of a chiral product, enabling enantioselective synthesis.

front: Why is it important that drugs containing chiral centres are produced as single enantiomers rather than racemic mixtures?
back: The two enantiomers of a drug can have very different biological activities. One may be **therapeutic** while the other is inactive or even **harmful**. Using a single enantiomer increases effectiveness, reduces side effects and can halve the patient dosage.

front:
**True or False?**

Conventional organic synthesis of a chiral drug always produces a single enantiomer.
back:
**False.**

Conventional organic synthesis produces a racemic mixture containing equal amounts of both enantiomers. Chiral catalysts or enzymes are needed to produce a single enantiomer.

front: An organometallic **..........** catalyst is used in the production of naproxen, directing synthesis towards the enantiomer that treats **..........** .
back: An organometallic **ruthenium** catalyst is used in the production of naproxen, directing synthesis towards the enantiomer that treats **arthritis**.

front: Define **stereoselectivity**.
back: A **stereoselectivity** is the preference of a reaction to produce one stereoisomer (enantiomer) over the other, often due to the specific geometry of a catalyst or enzyme binding site.

front: What are two advantages of using enzymes instead of conventional synthetic routes for producing pure drug enantiomers?
back:
1. Enzymes are highly **stereoselective**, producing only one enantiomer due to their specific active site geometry.
2. Enzyme-based synthesis is a **greener process**, involving fewer steps than conventional synthetic routes.

front:
**True or False?**

Enzymes used in drug synthesis must be mixed into the final product because they cannot be separated from it.
back:
**False.**

Enzymes are fixed on inert supports, allowing reactants to pass over them. The enzymes remain on the support and do not need to be separated from the product.

front: Separating a racemic mixture into pure single enantiomers reduces patient **..........** by half, because the pure enantiomer is more **..........** than the mixture.
back: Separating a racemic mixture into pure single enantiomers reduces patient **dosage** by half, because the pure enantiomer is more **potent** than the mixture.

front: What is a disadvantage of using enzymes to produce pure enantiomers compared to using synthetic chiral catalysts?
back: Enzymes can be **expensive to isolate** from living organisms. This has driven research into synthetic enzymes as alternatives, though enzyme-based routes do offer advantages such as fewer steps and greener chemistry.

front: Define **Friedel-Crafts reaction**.
back: A **Friedel-Crafts reaction** is an electrophilic substitution reaction of a benzene ring with a halogenoalkane (alkylation) or an acyl chloride (acylation) in the presence of an anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to nitrate benzene?
back: Benzene is mixed with concentrated nitric acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>) and concentrated sulfuric acid (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) at a temperature between 25 and 60°C. The H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> generates the **NO**<sub>**2**</sub><sup>**+**</sup>** electrophile**.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrogenation of benzene is a substitution reaction that preserves the aromatic ring.
back:
**False.**

Hydrogenation is an addition reaction that destroys the aromatic stabilisation of the benzene ring, producing cyclohexane.

front: In Friedel-Crafts alkylation, benzene reacts with a **..........** in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> to substitute an **..........** group onto the ring.
back: In Friedel-Crafts alkylation, benzene reacts with a **chloroalkane** in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> to substitute an **alkyl** group onto the ring.

front: What product is formed when alkyl side-chains in alkylarenes are completely oxidised?
back: The alkyl side-chains are oxidised to **carboxylic acid groups**. For example, ethylbenzene treated with hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> followed by acidification gives benzoic acid.

front:
**True or False?**

Alkylarenes are halogenated at the 2 and 4 positions because alkyl groups are electron-withdrawing.
back:
**False.**

Alkyl groups are electron-donating, not electron-withdrawing. They push electron density into the ring, activating the 2 and 4 positions towards electrophilic attack.

front: Define **acyl group**.
back: An **acyl group** is an alkyl group containing a carbonyl (C=O) group, with the general formula RCO–. It is introduced into a benzene ring by Friedel-Crafts acylation.

front: The complete oxidation of alkylarenes is carried out using hot, alkaline <u>          </u> followed by acidification with dilute <u>          </u>.
back: The complete oxidation of alkylarenes is carried out using hot, alkaline **KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub> followed by acidification with dilute **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub>.

front: What catalyst and conditions are required for the hydrogenation of benzene?
back: Benzene is heated with hydrogen gas in the presence of a nickel or platinum catalyst to form **cyclohexane**. This is an **addition reaction** that destroys the aromaticity of the ring.

front: Define **halogen carrier**.
back: A **halogen carrier** is an anhydrous Lewis acid catalyst (such as AlCl<sub>3</sub> or AlBr<sub>3</sub>) used in the halogenation of arenes. It accepts a lone pair from the halogen molecule to generate the electrophilic halogen cation (e.g. Cl<sup>+</sup> or Br<sup>+</sup>).

front: What are the three steps of electrophilic substitution in arenes?
back:
1. **Generation of the electrophile** (in situ from appropriate reagents).
2. **Electrophilic attack**: a pair of electrons from the benzene ring is donated to the electrophile, disrupting aromaticity.
3. **Regeneration of aromaticity**: heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond returns electrons to the π system.

front:
**True or False?**

During electrophilic attack on benzene, the aromaticity of the ring is maintained throughout the reaction.
back:
**False.**

Aromaticity is temporarily lost during electrophilic attack. The ring only has four π electrons and carries a positive charge spread over five carbons. Aromaticity is restored only in the final step by heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond.

front: The NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile used in nitration is generated by reacting concentrated **..........** with concentrated **..........** .
back: The NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile used in nitration is generated by reacting concentrated **HNO**<sub>**3**</sub> with concentrated **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub>.

front: How is the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile generated for the bromination of benzene?
back: Bromine forms a **dative bond** with the AlBr<sub>3</sub> halogen carrier by donating a lone pair from one of its bromine atoms into an empty 3p orbital of AlBr<sub>3</sub>. This polarises the Br–Br bond and generates **Br**<sup>**+**</sup> in situ.

front: Define **heterolytic cleavage**.
back: A **heterolytic cleavage** is the breaking of a covalent bond in which both electrons in the bond go to one of the two atoms, generating ions rather than radicals.

front:
**True or False?**

Arenes predominantly undergo addition reactions because the π electrons are easily available for attack.
back:
**False.**

Although arenes are electron-rich, they predominantly undergo substitution reactions because addition would destroy the thermodynamically stable delocalised aromatic π system. Substitution restores aromaticity.

front: During the halogenation of benzene, the halogen molecule forms a **..........** bond with the AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst by donating a lone pair into an empty **..........** orbital.
back: During the halogenation of benzene, the halogen molecule forms a **dative** bond with the AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst by donating a lone pair into an empty **3p** orbital.

front: Why does hydrogenation of benzene lead to a less stable product than benzene itself?
back: Hydrogenation is an addition reaction that completely destroys the **aromatic stabilisation** of benzene. Cyclohexane lacks the delocalised π system, so it is energetically less stable than benzene.

front: Define **free-radical substitution**.
back: A **free-radical substitution** is a chain reaction mechanism in which radicals (species with unpaired electrons) react with a substrate, typically initiated by UV light, resulting in substitution of a hydrogen atom.

front: What conditions direct halogenation to the aromatic ring rather than the side chain in alkylarenes?
back: Halogenation occurs in the aromatic ring when a halogen and anhydrous **halogen carrier catalyst** (such as AlBr<sub>3</sub> or AlCl<sub>3</sub>) are used. The catalyst generates the electrophile for electrophilic substitution.

front:
**True or False?**

Halogenation of the side chain of an alkylarene requires an anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
back:
**False.**

Side-chain halogenation is a free-radical substitution reaction requiring the halogen to be passed into the boiling alkylarene under UV light. No AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst is needed.

front: Aryl halides are less reactive than halogenoalkanes because the carbon–halogen bond in aryl halides has a partial **..........** character due to overlap of the halogen lone pair with the benzene **..........** system.
back: Aryl halides are less reactive than halogenoalkanes because the carbon–halogen bond in aryl halides has a partial **double bond** character due to overlap of the halogen lone pair with the benzene **π** system.

front: What happens when excess halogen is used in the side-chain halogenation of an alkylarene?
back: With excess halogen, **all hydrogen atoms** on the alkyl side-chain are progressively replaced by halogen atoms. No substitution occurs in the benzene ring under these conditions.

front:
**True or False?**

The carbon–halogen bond in an aryl halide is stronger than in a halogenoalkane.
back:
**True.**

The lone pairs on the halogen in an aryl halide partially overlap with the benzene π system, giving the C–X bond partial double bond character and making it stronger and harder to break than the C–X bond in a halogenoalkane.

front: Define **aryl halide**.
back: An **aryl halide** is an organic compound in which a halogen atom is bonded directly to a benzene ring. Aryl halides are formed by the electrophilic substitution of arenes with halogens.

front: Halogenation of an alkylarene in the side chain is initiated by **..........** light and proceeds via a **..........** mechanism.
back: Halogenation of an alkylarene in the side chain is initiated by **UV** light and proceeds via a **free-radical substitution** mechanism.

front: Why does the partial overlap of halogen lone pairs with the benzene π system affect the reactivity of aryl halides?
back: The lone pair overlap strengthens the C–X bond by giving it **partial double bond character**. This makes the bond harder to break, so aryl halides do not readily undergo nucleophilic substitution unlike halogenoalkanes.

front: Define **electron-donating group**.
back: An **electron-donating group** is a substituent that pushes electron density into the benzene ring, making it more reactive towards electrophilic substitution and directing incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and/or 6 positions.

front: Where does bromination occur on nitrobenzene, and why?
back: Bromination of nitrobenzene occurs at the **3 and/or 5 positions**. The nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) is electron-withdrawing, removing electron density from the ring and directing the incoming Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile to the 3 and 5 positions.

front:
**True or False?**

Electron-withdrawing groups increase the reactivity of a benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution.
back:
**False.**

Electron-withdrawing groups remove electron density from the π system, deactivating the ring and making it less reactive towards electrophilic substitution.

front: Electron-donating substituents (e.g. –R, –OH, –NH<sub>2</sub>) direct electrophilic attack to the **..........** positions, while electron-withdrawing substituents (e.g. –NO<sub>2</sub>, –COOH) direct attack to the **..........** positions.
back: Electron-donating substituents (e.g. –R, –OH, –NH<sub>2</sub>) direct electrophilic attack to the **2, 4 and/or 6** positions, while electron-withdrawing substituents (e.g. –NO<sub>2</sub>, –COOH) direct attack to the **3 and/or 5** positions.

front: Define **electron-withdrawing group**.
back: An **electron-withdrawing group** is a substituent that removes electron density from the benzene ring, deactivating it towards electrophilic substitution and directing incoming electrophiles to the 3 and/or 5 positions.

front: What two products are formed when methylbenzene is brominated, and what directs the substitution to those positions?
back: 2-bromomethylbenzene and 4-bromomethylbenzene are formed. The methyl group is electron-donating, pushing electron density into the ring and activating the **2 and 4 positions** towards the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile.

front:
**True or False?**

The –NH<sub>2</sub> group directs electrophilic substitution to the 3 and 5 positions of a benzene ring.
back:
**False.**

The –NH<sub>2</sub> group is an electron-donating substituent that activates the ring and directs electrophilic attack to the 2, 4 and/or 6 positions.

front: The –COR group is an electron-**..........** substituent that **..........** the benzene ring to electrophilic attack.
back: The –COR group is an electron-**withdrawing** substituent that **deactivates** the benzene ring to electrophilic attack.

front: How does an electron-donating group affect the position of electrophilic substitution on a benzene ring?
back: An electron-donating group increases electron density in the ring and activates it towards electrophilic substitution. It directs the incoming electrophile preferentially to the **2, 4 and/or 6 positions** relative to itself.

front: Define **halogenoarene**.
back: A **halogenoarene** is an aromatic compound in which one or more halogen atoms are bonded directly to the benzene ring. They are also called aryl halides.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to produce chlorobenzene from benzene?
back: Chlorine gas is bubbled into benzene at room temperature in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst. The AlCl<sub>3</sub> generates the **Cl**<sup>**+**</sup>** electrophile**, which attacks the benzene ring in an electrophilic substitution reaction.

front:
**True or False?**

The chlorination of benzene requires UV light to generate the electrophile.
back:
**False.**

The chlorination of benzene uses an anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst (halogen carrier) to generate the Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile. UV light is used for free-radical side-chain halogenation, not ring halogenation.

front: In the chlorination of benzene, the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst generates the **..........** electrophile. After electrophilic attack, a **..........** atom is eliminated to restore aromaticity.
back: In the chlorination of benzene, the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst generates the **Cl**<sup>**+**</sup> electrophile. After electrophilic attack, a **hydrogen** atom is eliminated to restore aromaticity.

front: Why does chlorination of methylbenzene give two products rather than one?
back: The methyl group is a **2,4-directing** electron-donating group that activates the 2 and 4 positions on the ring. Electrophilic substitution therefore occurs at both positions, giving 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene.

front:
**True or False?**

In the presence of excess chlorine, chlorination of methylbenzene can also occur at the 6 position.
back:
**True.**

With excess chlorine, substitution can additionally occur at the 6 position, since the methyl group activates the 2, 4 and 6 positions by electron donation.

front: Define **bromobenzene**.
back: A **bromobenzene** is a halogenoarene produced by the electrophilic substitution of benzene with bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) in the presence of anhydrous AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst.

front: The role of the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst in the chlorination of benzene is to generate the **..........** by reacting with Cl<sub>2</sub>, and it is described as a **..........** .
back: The role of the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst in the chlorination of benzene is to generate the **electrophile (Cl**<sup>**+**</sup>**)** by reacting with Cl<sub>2</sub>, and it is described as a **halogen carrier**.

front: What is restored at the end of the electrophilic substitution of benzene with chlorine, and how does this happen?
back: **Aromaticity is restored**. A hydrogen atom is removed in the second stage of the reaction (heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond), returning the bonding electrons to the benzene π system and regenerating the delocalised ring.

front: Define **partial double bond character**.
back: A **partial double bond character** is a property of a bond that has intermediate character between a single and a double bond, arising from electron delocalisation. In halogenoarenes, the C–X bond has partial double bond character due to lone pair overlap with the benzene π system.

front: Why are halogenoarenes much less reactive than halogenoalkanes?
back: In halogenoarenes, a lone pair on the halogen overlaps with the benzene π system, giving the C–X bond **partial double bond character**. This strengthens the bond and makes it very difficult to break, so nucleophilic substitution does not readily occur.

front:
**True or False?**

Chlorobenzene undergoes nucleophilic substitution readily at room temperature.
back:
**False.**

Chlorobenzene does not readily undergo nucleophilic substitution. Extremely harsh conditions (200°C and 200 atm pressure) are needed to replace the chlorine with a nucleophile such as OH<sup>-</sup>.

front: In halogenoarenes, delocalisation of a lone pair on the halogen over the benzene ring causes additional **..........** of the system and **..........** the carbon–halogen bond.
back: In halogenoarenes, delocalisation of a lone pair on the halogen over the benzene ring causes additional **stabilisation** of the system and **strengthens** the carbon–halogen bond.

front: How does chloroethane (a halogenoalkane) undergo nucleophilic substitution, and why is this different for chlorobenzene?
back: In chloroethane, the carbon bonded to chlorine is slightly positive, so a **nucleophile** such as OH<sup>-</sup> attacks and forms a covalent bond, displacing Cl<sup>-</sup>. In chlorobenzene, **lone pair delocalisation** into the ring strengthens the C–Cl bond so much that a nucleophile cannot break it under normal conditions.

front:
**True or False?**

The lone pair on the halogen in a halogenoarene interacts with the σ framework of the benzene ring.
back:
**False.**

The lone pair on the halogen interacts with the **π system** of the benzene ring, not the σ framework. This overlap gives the C–X bond partial double bond character.

front: Define **chlorobenzene**.
back: A **chlorobenzene** is a halogenoarene formed by the electrophilic substitution of benzene with chlorine using an AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst. It is very unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution due to the partial double bond character of its C–Cl bond.

front: To replace the chlorine in chlorobenzene by nucleophilic substitution, conditions of **..........** °C and **..........** atmospheres are required.
back: To replace the chlorine in chlorobenzene by nucleophilic substitution, conditions of **200** °C and **200** atmospheres are required.

front: Explain why the unreactivity of halogenoarenes can be attributed to delocalisation.
back: A lone pair on the halogen delocalises into the benzene π system, providing additional stabilisation of the whole molecule and giving the C–X bond **partial double bond character**. This strengthens the bond, making it harder to break. The result is that halogenoarenes are much less reactive than halogenoalkanes.

front: Define **acyl chloride**.
back: An **acyl chloride** is an organic compound containing a -COCl functional group, where the carbonyl carbon is electron-deficient and susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

front: Why is forming an ester from an acyl chloride more effective than using a carboxylic acid?
back: Acyl chlorides are **more reactive** so the ester forms faster, and the reaction **goes to completion** so the maximum yield of ester is produced.

front:
**True or False?**

Acyl chlorides react with alcohols vigorously, producing white fumes of HCl gas.
back:
**True.**

The C-Cl bond breaks during nucleophilic attack by the alcohol's -OH group, releasing HCl as white fumes.

front: When an acyl chloride reacts with an alcohol, the -OH group acts as a **..........**  and attacks the carbonyl carbon to substitute the **..........**  atom, forming an ester.
back: When an acyl chloride reacts with an alcohol, the -OH group acts as a **nucleophile** and attacks the carbonyl carbon to substitute the **chlorine** atom, forming an ester.

front: What conditions are required for an acyl chloride to react with phenol to form an ester?
back: A **base** (e.g. NaOH) is required. The base deprotonates phenol to form the **phenoxide ion**, which is a better nucleophile and can attack the carbonyl carbon. The reaction proceeds at **room temperature**.

front:
**True or False?**

Phenol reacts with acyl chlorides under the same conditions as aliphatic alcohols.
back:
**False.**

Aliphatic alcohols react vigorously with acyl chlorides at room temperature **without a base**. Phenol also reacts at room temperature but requires a **base** (e.g. NaOH) to form the **phenoxide ion** before nucleophilic attack can occur.

front: **phenoxide ion**
back: A **phenoxide ion** is the conjugate base of phenol, formed when phenol is deprotonated by a base. It is a better nucleophile than phenol because the negative charge makes the oxygen more electron-rich.

front: What is the mechanism type for the reaction of acyl chlorides with alcohols or phenols?
back: **Addition-elimination**: the nucleophile (alcohol or phenoxide) adds across the C=O bond, then HCl is eliminated to form the ester.

front: In the reaction of an acyl chloride with phenol, a **..........**  must first form the **..........**  ion, which then attacks the carbonyl carbon.
back: In the reaction of an acyl chloride with phenol, a **base** must first form the **phenoxide** ion, which then attacks the carbonyl carbon.

front: **diazonium salt**
back: A **diazonium salt** is an unstable organic compound containing an -N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> group, formed by reacting phenylamine with nitrous acid below 10 °C.

front: What reagents are used to prepare nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) in the first step of phenol production?
back: Sodium nitrite (NaNO<sub>2</sub>) and dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) are mixed while keeping the temperature below 10 °C using ice.

front:
**True or False?**

Benzenediazonium chloride is a stable compound that can be stored at room temperature.
back:
**False.**

Benzenediazonium chloride is very unstable and thermally decomposes when heated, which is why the temperature must be kept below 10 °C during its formation.

front: In step 2 of phenol production, phenylamine reacts with **..........**  to form an unstable **..........**  salt.
back: In step 2 of phenol production, phenylamine reacts with **HNO**<sub>**2**</sub> to form an unstable **diazonium** salt.

front: What happens in step 3 of phenol production from phenylamine?
back: The diazonium salt is heated and undergoes thermal decomposition to form phenol.

front:
**True or False?**

Phenols are characterised by an -OH group attached directly to a benzene ring.
back:
**True.**

The -OH group bonded directly to the benzene ring is the defining structural feature of phenols.

front: Why must ice be used during the preparation of nitrous acid in phenol production?
back: Nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) is so unstable that the temperature must be kept below 10 °C to prevent it from decomposing before it can react with phenylamine.

front: Phenol is produced from phenylamine by first forming **..........**  acid, then reacting it with phenylamine to give a **..........**  salt, which is then heated.
back: Phenol is produced from phenylamine by first forming **nitrous** acid, then reacting it with phenylamine to give a **diazonium** salt, which is then heated.

front: **phenol**
back: **Phenol** is an organic compound in which a hydroxyl (-OH) group is bonded directly to a benzene ring, giving it weakly acidic properties.

front: Define **azo compound**.
back: An **azo compound** is an organic compound in which two benzene rings are linked by a nitrogen bridge (-N=N-), formed from the reaction of a diazonium ion with phenol in alkaline solution.

front: Why does phenol react more readily with electrophiles than benzene does?
back: One of the **lone pairs** on the oxygen atom in the -OH group overlaps with the π bonding system of the ring, increasing electron density and making the ring more susceptible to **electrophilic attack**.

front:
**True or False?**

Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
back:
**True.**

The -OH group activates the ring so strongly that phenol decolourises orange bromine water without a catalyst, forming a white precipitate.

front: Phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide in an acid-base reaction to form a **..........**  salt and **..........** .
back: Phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide in an acid-base reaction to form **sodium phenoxide** salt and **water**.

front: What positions does the -OH group in phenol direct incoming electrophiles to?
back: The -OH group directs electrophiles to the **2, 4, and 6 positions** on the benzene ring.

front:
**True or False?**

Molten phenol reacts with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas and a soluble salt.
back:
**True.**

This is an acid-base reaction. Phenol acts as the acid, donating a proton to sodium, producing sodium phenoxide (a soluble salt) and H<sub>2</sub> gas.

front: What colour is the product formed when phenol reacts with a cold diazonium ion in alkaline solution?
back: A **yellow-orange** solution or precipitate is formed, which is an **azo compound** containing two benzene rings linked by a nitrogen bridge.

front: Phenol undergoes **..........**  with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature to give a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and **..........** .
back: Phenol undergoes **nitration** with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature to give a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and **4-nitrophenol**.

front: Define **electrophilic substitution**.
back: **Electrophilic substitution** is a reaction in which an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring, leaving the ring structure intact.

front: Define **phenoxide ion**.
back: A **phenoxide ion** is the conjugate base of phenol, formed when phenol loses a proton. The negative charge is delocalised across the entire ion, stabilising it.

front: Why is phenol a weak acid even though it contains an -OH group similar to alcohols?
back: One of the lone pairs on the oxygen atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring. This stabilises the phenoxide ion formed, making phenol more likely to lose a proton than gain one.

front:
**True or False?**

Phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol.
back:
**True.**

Phenol has a pKa of 10 while ethanol has a pKa of 16. The lower pKa of phenol means it dissociates more readily and is a stronger acid.

front: In the phenoxide ion, the negative charge is **..........**  over the entire ion, which means H<sup>+</sup> ions are less likely to **..........**  the phenol molecule.
back: In the phenoxide ion, the negative charge is **delocalised** over the entire ion, which means H<sup>+</sup> ions are less likely to **reform** the phenol molecule.

front: Place ethanol, water and phenol in order of increasing acid strength and give their approximate pKa values.
back: Ethanol (pKa 16) < water (pKa 15.7) < phenol (pKa 10). Phenol is the strongest acid of the three.

front:
**True or False?**

The ethoxide ion is a weaker base than the phenoxide ion.
back:
**False.**

The ethyl group donates electron density to the oxygen in the ethoxide ion, making it more available to accept a proton. The ethoxide ion is therefore a stronger base than the phenoxide ion.

front: Why does the dissociation equilibrium of phenol lie further to the right compared to ethanol?
back: The phenoxide ion is more stable than the ethoxide ion because the negative charge is delocalised across the benzene ring. This makes phenol more likely to donate a proton.

front: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because the **..........**  ion formed is stabilised by **..........**  of charge over the aromatic ring.
back: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because the **phenoxide** ion formed is stabilised by **delocalisation** of charge over the aromatic ring.

front: Define **pKa**.
back: **pKa** is a measure of acid strength: the smaller the pKa value, the stronger the acid and the more readily it donates a proton.

front: Define **activating group**.
back: An **activating group** is a substituent that increases the electron density of an aromatic ring, making it more reactive towards electrophilic substitution.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to nitrate phenol, and how do these differ from benzene?
back: Phenol only requires dilute nitric acid at room temperature. Benzene requires a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, refluxed between 25 °C and 60 °C.

front:
**True or False?**

Phenol reacts with bromine water in the absence of a catalyst to give a white precipitate.
back:
**True.**

Unlike benzene, which needs pure bromine and an AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst, phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without any catalyst.

front: The -OH group in phenol is **..........**  and directs incoming electrophiles to the **..........**  and **..........**  positions.
back: The -OH group in phenol is **electron-donating** and directs incoming electrophiles to the **2, 4** and **6** positions.

front: What product forms when phenol is treated with concentrated nitric acid instead of dilute nitric acid?
back: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol is formed when concentrated nitric acid is used.

front:
**True or False?**

The lone pair on the oxygen atom in phenol overlaps with the π system of the benzene ring, increasing electron density in the ring.
back:
**True.**

This overlap delocalises one of the oxygen lone pairs into the ring, activating it towards electrophilic substitution and directing electrophiles to the 2, 4, and 6 positions.

front: Why can phenol be brominated using bromine water, while benzene requires pure bromine and a catalyst?
back: The -OH group in phenol donates electron density into the ring, increasing it sufficiently to react with bromine water. Benzene is less electron-rich and requires a catalyst to polarise the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule.

front: Bromination of benzene requires **..........**  bromine and an **..........**  catalyst, but phenol only needs bromine water at room temperature.
back: Bromination of benzene requires **pure** bromine and an **AlBr**<sub>**3**</sub> catalyst, but phenol only needs bromine water at room temperature.

front: Define **directing effect**.
back: A **directing effect** is the influence a substituent has on determining which positions on an aromatic ring are attacked by an incoming electrophile during electrophilic substitution.

front: Define **phenolic compound**.
back: A **phenolic compound** is any organic molecule that contains a phenol functional group (-OH bonded directly to a benzene ring).

front: What structural feature makes 1-naphthol a phenolic compound?
back: 1-naphthol contains an -OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring. The benzene ring is itself fused to a second benzene ring.

front:
**True or False?**

In 1-naphthol, electrophilic substitution can occur at the 6 position.
back:
**False.**

Substitution at position 6 is not possible because there is no hydrogen atom on that carbon. It is bonded to a carbon atom of the second benzene ring.

front: In 1-naphthol, the -OH group is **..........**  and directs electrophiles to the **..........**  and/or **..........**  positions.
back: In 1-naphthol, the -OH group is **electron-donating** and directs electrophiles to the **2** and/or **4** positions.

front: How does 1-naphthol react with electrophiles compared with phenol?
back: 1-naphthol reacts in the same way as phenol. The -OH group activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs incoming electrophiles to the 2 and/or 4 positions.

front:
**True or False?**

The -OH group in 1-naphthol activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution.
back:
**True.**

Just as in phenol, the -OH group in 1-naphthol donates electron density into the ring, making it more reactive towards electrophilic attack.

front: What is the structural relationship between 1-naphthol and phenol?
back: 1-naphthol has a phenol group (-OH attached to a benzene ring) which is fused to a second benzene ring, making it a bicyclic phenolic compound.

front: 1-naphthol contains a **..........**  group attached to another **..........**  ring, and undergoes electrophilic substitution in a similar way to **..........** .
back: 1-naphthol contains a **phenol** group attached to another **benzene** ring, and undergoes electrophilic substitution in a similar way to **phenol**.

front: Define **1-naphthol**.
back: **1-naphthol** is a phenolic compound consisting of a phenol group fused to a second benzene ring. It reacts like phenol in electrophilic substitution, with substitution directed to the 2 and/or 4 positions.

front: Define **benzoic acid**.
back: **Benzoic acid** is the simplest aromatic carboxylic acid, with the molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH. It can be produced by oxidising alkylbenzenes.

front: What reagent is used to oxidise methylbenzene to benzoic acid, and what conditions are required?
back: **Hot alkaline KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub> is used as the oxidising agent. The mixture is heated under reflux, then acidified with dilute acid to protonate the product and form benzoic acid.

front:
**True or False?**

During the oxidation of methylbenzene with alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, the purple colour disappears as Mn<sup>7+</sup> is reduced to Mn<sup>4+</sup>.
back:
**True.**

The purple colour of permanganate fades as Mn<sup>7+</sup> is reduced to Mn<sup>4+</sup>, and a brown precipitate of MnO<sub>2</sub> forms.

front: The alkyl side-chain of an alkylbenzene is oxidised to a **..........**  group by hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>. The mixture is then acidified to produce a **..........**  acid.
back: The alkyl side-chain of an alkylbenzene is oxidised to a **carboxylic acid** group by hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>. The mixture is then acidified to produce a **benzoic** acid.

front: Why is the reaction mixture acidified after oxidising methylbenzene with alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
back: Acidification protonates the organic product to form the final benzoic acid. Under alkaline conditions, the product exists as a **carboxylate salt** rather than the free acid.

front:
**True or False?**

Benzoic acid and its derivatives can be used as reagents in the synthesis of esters.
back:
**True.**

The revision note states that benzoic acids and their derivatives are often used as reagents in ester synthesis.

front: What visible change is observed in the KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution and what precipitate forms during the oxidation of an alkylbenzene?
back: The purple solution decolourises as Mn<sup>7+</sup> is reduced, and a brown precipitate of MnO<sub>2</sub> is formed.

front: Benzoic acid is produced from methylbenzene by heating under **..........**  with hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, then acidifying with **..........**  acid.
back: Benzoic acid is produced from methylbenzene by heating under **reflux** with hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, then acidifying with **dilute** acid.

front: Define **alkylbenzene**.
back: An **alkylbenzene** is a compound consisting of a benzene ring with one or more alkyl side-chains. The side-chain can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid group using hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

front: Define **acyl chloride**.
back: An **acyl chloride** is a compound with a -COCl functional group. It is more reactive than the corresponding carboxylic acid and is used as a starting material in the synthesis of esters and amides.

front: Name three reagents that can be used to convert a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride.
back: **PCl**<sub>**5**</sub> (solid), **PCl**<sub>**3**</sub> (liquid) with heat, and **SOCl**<sub>**2**</sub> (liquid).

front:
**True or False?**

Methanoic acid can be oxidised further to carbon dioxide using Tollens' reagent.
back:
**True.**

Methanoic acid is a strong reducing agent. It can be oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution.

front: When methanoic acid is warmed with Fehling's solution, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Cu<sup>+</sup>, which precipitates as **..........**  Cu<sub>2</sub>O.
back: When methanoic acid is warmed with Fehling's solution, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Cu<sup>+</sup>, which precipitates as **red** Cu<sub>2</sub>O.

front: What is observed when ethanedioic acid is oxidised by warm acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
back: The purple KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution turns colourless as Mn<sup>7+</sup> is reduced to Mn<sup>2+</sup>, and carbon dioxide is produced.

front:
**True or False?**

All carboxylic acids can be further oxidised by mild oxidising agents such as Fehling's solution.
back:
**False.**

Only methanoic acid (and ethanedioic acid, which requires strong oxidising agents) can be further oxidised. Most carboxylic acids are not oxidised by mild reagents like Fehling's solution.

front: Why are acyl chlorides more useful than carboxylic acids in ester synthesis?
back: Acyl chlorides are **more reactive** so the reaction is faster, and the reaction **goes to completion** so the yield of ester is higher. Reactions with carboxylic acids are slower and reach an equilibrium.

front: Acyl chlorides can be prepared from carboxylic acids using solid **..........**  or liquid **..........**  or liquid SOCl<sub>2</sub>.
back: Acyl chlorides can be prepared from carboxylic acids using solid **PCl**<sub>**5**</sub> or liquid **PCl**<sub>**3**</sub> or liquid SOCl<sub>2</sub>.

front: Define **ethanedioic acid**.
back: **Ethanedioic acid** is a dicarboxylic acid that can be further oxidised to carbon dioxide by warm acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

front: Define **carboxylate ion**.
back: A **carboxylate ion** is the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid, formed when the O-H bond breaks. The negative charge is delocalised over both oxygen atoms of the -COO<sup>-</sup> group, stabilising the ion.

front: Place ethanol, phenol and ethanoic acid in order of increasing acid strength and give their approximate pKa values.
back: Ethanol (pKa 16) < phenol (pKa 10) < **ethanoic acid** (pKa 4.8). **Ethanoic acid** is the strongest acid of the three.

front:
**True or False?**

Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols because their carbonyl group weakens the O-H bond.
back:
**True.**

The carbonyl (C=O) group in carboxylic acids withdraws electron density from the O-H bond, weakening it so that the proton is lost more easily than in phenols or alcohols.

front: In alcohols, the alkyl group is **..........**  and donates electron density to the oxygen, making the **..........**  ion less stable than the phenoxide ion.
back: In alcohols, the alkyl group is **electron-donating** and donates electron density to the oxygen, making the **alkoxide** ion less stable than the phenoxide ion.

front: Why is the carboxylate ion more stable than the phenoxide ion?
back: In the carboxylate ion, the charge is delocalised onto an electronegative **carbonyl oxygen** atom, making the electrons less available for bonding with H<sup>+</sup>. In the **phenoxide ion**, the charge is spread over carbon atoms in the ring, which are less electronegative.

front:
**True or False?**

Alkoxide ions can delocalise their negative charge over a ring system.
back:
**False.**

Alkoxide ions lack an aromatic ring and cannot delocalise charge. The alkyl group actually donates electron density to the oxygen, concentrating charge rather than spreading it.

front: How does the carbonyl group in carboxylic acids affect the O-H bond?
back: The carbonyl group is **electron-withdrawing** and pulls electron density away from the O-H bond through the C-O bond, weakening the O-H bond so that the proton can be lost more easily.

front: Benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is a **..........**  acid than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8) because the benzene ring is **..........**  and stabilises the carboxylate ion.
back: Benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is a **stronger** acid than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8) because the benzene ring is **electron-withdrawing** and stabilises the carboxylate ion.

front: Define **alkoxide ion**.
back: An **alkoxide ion** is the conjugate base of an alcohol. The electron-donating alkyl group concentrates charge on the oxygen, making the alkoxide a strong base and the parent alcohol a very weak acid.

front: Define **electron-withdrawing group**.
back: An **electron-withdrawing group** is a substituent that pulls electron density away from the rest of the molecule, weakening the O-H bond in carboxylic acids and increasing their acid strength.

front: Why does chloroethanoic acid have a lower pKa than ethanoic acid?
back: The chlorine atom is **electron-withdrawing** and pulls electron density away from the -COOH group, weakening the O-H bond and further stabilising the **carboxylate ion** formed. This makes chloroethanoic acid a stronger acid.

front:
**True or False?**

Trichloroethanoic acid (pKa 0.6) is a stronger acid than chloroethanoic acid (pKa 2.9).
back:
**True.**

The three chlorine atoms in trichloroethanoic acid withdraw more electron density than one chlorine atom in chloroethanoic acid, weakening the O-H bond further and giving a lower pKa.

front: As the number of chlorine atoms on the carbon attached to -COOH increases, the O-H bond becomes **..........**  and the acid becomes **..........** .
back: As the number of chlorine atoms on the carbon attached to -COOH increases, the O-H bond becomes **weaker** and the acid becomes **stronger**.

front: Why is ethanoic acid the weakest acid in the series of chlorine-substituted ethanoic acids?
back: Ethanoic acid contains an **electron-donating** methyl group that strengthens the O-H bond and donates negative charge to the -COO<sup>-</sup> group, making it more likely to accept a proton and reform the acid.

front:
**True or False?**

Electron-withdrawing groups increase acid strength by destabilising the carboxylate ion.
back:
**False.**
